📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cleantechnica ↗ Open Full Page

Europe’s Modelled €5.70/kg Hydrogen Faces Industrial Buyers Who Can Afford Far Less

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (947 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, europe’s industrial hydrogen intends have a buyer problem.
  • The central 2050 scenario in my European hydrogen assessment puts on-site production at €5.70/kg.
  • At a factory using hydrogen for process heat, €5.70/kg is an expensive fuel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, europe’s industrial hydrogen intends have a buyer problem. A factory cannot make its products competitive by paying whatever a fresh hydrogen plant needs to recover its investment. Its maximum hydrogen price is set by the cost of making the same product, or delivering the same useful heat, another way.

The central 2050 scenario in my European hydrogen assessment puts on-site production at €5.70/kg. That starts with electricity at €60/MWh and 53 kWh of electricity per kilogram of hydrogen, so the electricity alone costs €3.18/kg. Electrolysers, capital recovery, maintenance, stack replacements, water and other plant costs bring the total to €5.70. Getting hydrogen to a customer can cost more.

At a factory using hydrogen for process heat, €5.70/kg is an expensive fuel. With 94% heating efficiency, delivering one MWh of useful heat requires roughly 31.9 kg of hydrogen. The fuel bill reaches €182/MWh before the burner, maintenance and other equipment costs. In the model’s central 2050 comparison, suitable direct-electric heating sets a hydrogen price ceiling of €2.07/kg. At that ceiling the same hydrogen heat costs about €66/MWh. The hydrogen production case overshoots the customer’s competitive input price by €3.63/kg.

The mismatch is not a prediction that hydrogen makers will never lower costs. It is the actual commercial test investors should apply before financing supply. Reducing the cost of production from €7 to €5 a kilogram achieves little if the relevant industrial customer can pay €2. Production-cost targets are meaningless without a corresponding market price ceiling.

Recent findings suggest that the International Energy Agency’s Global Hydrogen Review 2026 has made customer cost acceptability part of its assessment. Across most sector and region comparisons, the IEA finds maximum acceptable hydrogen prices below US$2/kg without policy support. Some incumbent-steel comparisons yield negative acceptable prices. The IEA examines a 2035 horizon and a different set of competitors; the same buyer-side arithmetic exposes the problem.

My TFIE Strategy Briefing assessment calculates the maximum hydrogen input price for industrial heat, ammonia and ironmaking and compares it with distinct European supply cases. It also links to the underlying European hydrogen research and interactive model.

Recent findings suggest that european ammonia illustrates how demand for a product differs from demand for European-made hydrogen. Ammonia remains necessary for fertilisers and industrial chemicals. The buyer’s real choice is where to produce it. In the central 2050 TFIE model, making qualifying green ammonia inside Europe can compete with imported green ammonia only when its hydrogen input costs roughly €2.62–€4.00/kg, depending on the origin and production route. The €5.70/kg onsite supply case misses those thresholds. Europe can keep consuming ammonia without building every electrolyser locally.

Ironmaking has a similar sourcing decision. The model’s hydrogen input-price ceiling versus qualifying imported hydrogen-reduced or hot-briquetted iron ranges from €2.28 to €4.45/kg. Against a European electrochemical iron process, the central ceiling is approximately €1.43/kg. Where enough suitable scrap can deliver the required steel grade, the hydrogen-based route can lose even at a zero price for hydrogen. Steel quality, industrial integration and the commercial maturity of electrochemical iron matter to those comparisons. They do not entitle a hydrogen supplier to ignore the alternatives.

Industry observers note that hydrogen used as a chemical reagent deserves a different assessment from hydrogen burned for heat. Chemical production may need the molecule. Industrial heating needs temperature, pressure, reliability and useful energy, all of which can be delivered directly from electricity for many applications. Manufacturing hydrogen from electricity and then burning it adds conversion losses and fuel-system costs before the plant receives the heat it needs.

In a recent development, the supply cases have defined boundaries. The central onsite cost is €5.70/kg. A generic delivery allowance takes that case to €6.95/kg. The model’s separately configured hub-and-pipeline case is €5.81/kg. Those are different cost structures, not interchangeable price quotes for the same customer. Even the favourable 2050 case, at €3.46/kg with its specified delivery allowance and €28/MWh electricity, clears some industrial thresholds but still misses others.

Policy can create demand that market prices do not support. Carbon pricing, procurement mandates, subsidies and carbon contracts for difference can raise willingness or obligation to pay. That may be a deliberate industrial or climate choice, but governments should disclose the premium, who will finance it and the contract duration. Describing a regulated purchase as competitive demand hides the cost rather than eliminating it.

The EU energy regulators’ market monitoring points in the same direction. ACER reported 4.2 GW of committed electrolyser capacity in November 2026, including operating plants, projects under construction and those with final investment decisions. Roughly 49% was associated with refining, where renewable-fuel mandates provide a strong demand signal. The remaining industrial sectors face a harder test when policy does not compel the same purchases.

It has been revealed that for lenders, the consequence is immediate. A proposed hydrogen plant costing €5/kg has no viable commercial case when its intended industrial buyer can afford €3/kg. A memorandum of understanding cannot close that €2/kg gap. Developers need buyers with enforceable contracts at prices that cover supply costs, lower production costs, or identified support durable enough to finance the difference.

It has been revealed that industrial and public procurement should start with the product the customer must deliver, calculate the best eligible competing route, and determine the maximum hydrogen price that route permits. Only then should investors consider electrolysers, pipelines and capacity targets. Suppliers do not set the market by drawing cheaper future cost curves. Industrial customers set the ceiling.

The full TFIE Briefing and open European hydrogen assessment contain the industrial route comparisons, scenario assumptions and research submitted to the European Commission. The next Briefing examines the competing routes for sourcing green ammonia and iron.

Wiz ties Microsoft Agent Framework package compromise to release pipeline certificate

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (935 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Microsoft Corp.’s official Python package for its Agent Framework artificial intelligence agent toolkit was compromised earlier this week, as an attacker published two malicious versions to the Python Package Index that were designed to steal cloud and developer credentials.
  • Industry observers note that the malicious versions, 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, were published on Tuesday through Microsoft’s own publisher account, giving them the appearance of a routine update to a package that sees close to 200,000 downloads a month.
  • Researchers at cloud security organization Wiz Inc.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 17:44 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

Microsoft Corp.’s official Python package for its Agent Framework artificial intelligence agent toolkit was compromised earlier this week, as an attacker published two malicious versions to the Python Package Index that were designed to steal cloud and developer credentials.

Industry observers note that the malicious versions, 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, were published on Tuesday through Microsoft’s own publisher account, giving them the appearance of a routine update to a package that sees close to 200,000 downloads a month. Both versions were pulled from PyPI within about an hour, but anyone who installed them in that window is at risk.

Researchers at cloud security organization Wiz Inc. have since found that the attacker appears to have gained publishing access using a client certificate and private key for Microsoft’s Engineering System Release Pipeline, an internal service the company uses to sign and publish packages. Address filtering on the service blocked the attacker’s first attempt from Amazon Web Services, according to Wiz, though the attacker was able to publish on a second try from Microsoft-owned address space.

Recent findings suggest that how the attacker obtained the credentials is not known. Microsoft had not responded to a request for comment from BleepingComputer as of Wednesday.

The researchers also observed part of the operation, as the attacker’s tooling was reporting its progress to the same public webhook it was using to collect stolen data. The tooling identified itself as Cairn, an open-source penetration-testing framework that uses AI.

The malware itself is delivered through a .pth file added to both releases, a type of file Python runs every time it starts, meaning the credential stealer runs even if the framework itself is never imported. The two versions also kept the genuine agent-framework-core 1.26.0 as a dependency, so the framework continued to work normally while the malware ran in the background.

Recent findings suggest that once running, the malware collects secrets from environment variables and from other running processes, along with credential files for services such as Azure, npm, Git, Docker and Hugging Face. It also requests Azure managed identity tokens for 12 resources, according to application security manufacturer Endor Labs Inc., with the second version adding requests for GitHub Actions tokens. The stolen data is then compressed, encoded and sent to a webhook.site address controlled by the attacker.

Researchers at malware tracking site OpenSourceMalware described the malware as a “focused credential and token stealer, not a remote access trojan,” noting that it does not install any persistence on infected systems.

Sources indicate that wiz’s analysis suggests the number of victims may be small, though it covers only the 50 requests the attacker’s free webhook.site account retained. Of those, 17 represented only three unique successful thefts of victim data, with the rest coming from the attacker’s own machines and from sandbox and security vendor scanning.

The incident is not the first this year involving an official Microsoft Python package. In May, Microsoft’s durabletask package was hijacked after its PyPI token was stolen in an attack that has been linked to TeamPCP, the group also behind the compromise of LiteLLM. Wiz says it has not linked the two incidents.

Anyone who installed either of the malicious versions is being urged to treat it as a credential compromise, according to researchers, who recommend rebuilding from version 1.26.0 and rotating any secrets the affected systems could access.

“A list of dependencies in production might show no trace of the framework, while a build runner could have installed it and been shut down before the alert arrived,” James Matchett, head of security at software supply chain security company Cloudsmith Ltd., told SiliconANGLE.

“If that runner had access to a deployment token, the team needs to know which version it installed and what the token could access,” he added.

#87937. Mazda Miata Engine Swaps Ranked Best To Worst (For Your Budget And Your Patience)

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1526 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Jalopnik ↗ Open Full Page

Mazda Miata Engine Swaps Ranked Best To Worst (For Your Budget And Your Patience)

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1526 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jalopnik has long maintained that the Mazda Miata is the answer to every question.
  • But Miata enthusiasts are a crafty bunch, and over the nameplate's 37-year history, their quest for more power has driven the development of camshafts, turbochargers, and, of course, engine swaps.
  • Not all swaps are created equal, though.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jalopnik has long maintained that the Mazda Miata is the answer to every question. What's the best affordable convertible? Miata. What if you want a fun commuter that's reliable and sips fuel? You should consider a Miata. What if you want a car to take off-road? Surprisingly, the Miata is the answer again. Emme Hall won her class in a Baja race with her off-road modified Miata. It's an excellent sports car, relatively cheap, abundant, and just plain fun. Over four generations, the only only real critique of the venerable roadster is that it's never been particularly quick in a straight line.

But Miata enthusiasts are a crafty bunch, and over the nameplate's 37-year history, their quest for more power has driven the development of camshafts, turbochargers, and, of course, engine swaps. Swaps are not for the faint of heart – they often consume a lot of time and capital — but they are a great way to add power without the complexities of a forced induction setup on the factory engine.

Not all swaps are created equal, though. For example, transplanting an engine from a newer Miata will be easier and cheaper than shoehorning a V8 into the engine bay. However, the V8 will net you way more power for the extra effort and money. There are so many Miata swaps out there — from Honda K24 four-cylinders to Toyota V12s — so we have compiled a helpful a list of engines that go in Miatas, organized from the cheapest and easiest to the most difficult and expensive.

The easiest Miata swaps involve upgrading to a larger Mazda motor within the same engine family. Early first-generation Miatas (1990 to 1993) were equipped with a 1.6-liter four-cylinder. Its output was a tepid 116 horsepower. Luckily, later first-generation cars (1994 to 1997) and all second-generation cars (1999 to 2005) came with a more powerful 1.8-liter four-cylinder that will bolt up to the factory transmission. Flyin' Miata sells an affordable kit that makes the swap to the 1994-to-1997 engine essentially plug-and-play. The later engines make more power, but they still require some effort to work in the 1.6 cars. To get the most power for your money and effort, look for a 2001-to-2005 Miata engine donor. They have variable valve timing and provide 142 horsepower .

Similarly, third-generation Miatas (2006 to 2015) have an easy path to more displacement and power. A 2.5-liter Duratec four-cylinder engine from a Ford Fusion, Mazda3, Mazda6, or Mercury Milan fits in place of the Miata's 2.0-liter four-cylinder with minimal effort. The larger engine is plentiful in junkyards and can be had for as cheap as $350. The swap isn't completely plug-and-play — the Miata's lower intake manifold needs to be modified to fit the 2.5 — but most of the 2.0-liter's accessories fit the larger engine without concern. A stock 2.5 makes about 10 more horsepower and 35 more pound-feet of torque over the factory Miata engine. But with upgraded cams and a freer-flowing exhaust, Grassroots Motorsports made 196 hp at the wheels with its 2.5 swap.

It has been revealed that under the hood, the Miata has never had much more than an economy-car four-cylinder turned sideways. By contrast, when Honda decided to make a roadster of its own, the automaker equipped it with the F20C four-cylinder — an engine with a 9,000-rpm redline that held the title for the most naturally aspirated horsepower per liter until the Ferrari 458 came along. Intrepid engine swappers may think a Miata with an F20C could be a good way to create a low-buck, bootleg S2000. But S2000 engines aren't exactly affordable or easy to come by.

Industry observers note that however, there is another Honda option that can rev almost as high as the F20C and makes similar power. Enter the K24, the budget friendly and readily available alternative. The K24, like its name might suggest, is a 2.4-liter four-cylinder with dual-overhead camshafts and Honda's i-VTEC system. The high performance variants of the engine found in the Acura TSX and Honda Civic Si make around 200 horsepower in factory trim. But the aftermarket for the engine is immense, and with the right combination of parts, the K24 has the potential to make nearly 300 hp without boost.

It has been revealed that although it was only available in front- and all-wheel-drive cars, tuners like KPower Industries recognized the engine's potential for rear-wheel-drive applications. As such, KPower Industries makes kits to swap a K24 into all four generations of Miatas. It's not a simple or cheap swap. Bits like a transmission adapter plate and a standalone ECU are needed to make it all work, and the most comprehensive kits start at around $6,000. But for a powerful, lightweight engine that doesn't mess with the balance of the Miata chassis, the juice is worth the squeeze.

The next rung on the Miata-swap ladder is the V6. A V6 swap is an exercise in more — more cylinders, more power, more effort, and more money. There are three V6 engines that have readily available Miata swap kits: the 3.5-liter Honda J35 found in the Odyssey and various Acuras, the direct-injected 3.6-liter GM LFX found in the Chevy Camaro and Cadillac CTS, and the 3.0-liter Jaguar AJ30 V6 found in the S-type and XJ. Each option has an aluminum block and heads, and depending on the variant, outputs roughly 40 to 100 more horsepower than a stock K24.

Sources indicate that no matter what engine you choose, the kits are not cheap. Luckily, with a kit, you don't have to fabricate your own front subframe, motor mounts, and other swap-related parts. The Honda J35 kit from Mini Tec is the most affordable at $3,350, and it utilizes the factory Miata transmission and differential. But that doesn't include any provisions for the cooling, power steering, and fueling systems. The next kit on the list is the $7,260 GM LFX V6 conversion from V8Roadsters, which requires a Camaro transmission and other GM donor parts. This adds more complexity to the swap, but the GM parts are more durable than the factory Miata stuff. Rocketeer Cars takes the most comprehensive approach to V6 swaps. It will sell you everything you need for the conversion, including a refreshed Jaguar AJ30 V6. But that will set you back roughly $22,040. If you are going to spend all of that money on a V6, you might as well go for the gusto and consider our next swap option.

Recent findings suggest that if the Miata is the universal answer to any sports car question, the Chevy LS is the the answer for any engine swap inquiry. The V8 LS-series engines are still such a popular swap for a reason. They're compact, powerful, readily available in junkyards, and have massive aftermarket support. The LS engine is available in many configurations, from 4.8-liter truck engines to 7.0-liter sports car screamers. Even the wimpiest 4.8-liter LS can make 400 horsepower without much effort. That type of power is a tantalizing prospect for those looking to make a modern version of a Shelby Cobra with a Miata. Fortunately, for those with enough capital and bravery, the significant V8 can be stuffed into every generation of Miata. Although Colorado-based tuner Flyin' Miata stopped doing V8 swaps years ago, other manufactures like Monster Miata and V8Roadsters will sell you the parts to roll your own.

According to recent reports, there are many tradeoffs involved in putting an LS in a Miata, first of which is the car's balance. Monster Miata notes the weight distribution moves from a perfect 50/50 to a nose-heavy 53/47 with a big V8 under the hood. Also, the rest of the Miata's driveline can't hold up to V8 power, so it needs to be swapped as well. You'll need parts like a T-56 six-speed transmission, fresh driveshaft, and a differential from a fith-gen Camaro. Costs are highly variable depending on which engine you choose, but they generally fall somewhere around $20,000 for the average completed swap.

According to recent reports, A Miata with more than eight cylinders is like an automotive cryptid. There's evidence that it exists, but it can only be found in the murky depths of internet forums and YouTube. During our dive into the internet swamps, we found a Miata with a Viper V10, one with a Jaguar V12, and another with a Toyota 1GZFE V12 from a Toyota Century.

Sources indicate that the efficacy of these swaps is questionable, as there are no off-the-shelf kits for them. And more cylinders means more weight over the nose of the Miata, even further messing up the roadster's weight distribution compared to an LS. Plus, an LS can make just as much power or more power than the engines above. The LS also fits in the engine bay a whole lot better. The guy who did the Jaguar V12 swap said he had to cut the firewall and move it 6 inches back. But if you're crazy enough to try one of these swaps, you'll certainly have the only Miata at the Cars and Coffee with more than eight cylinders.

#87935. EV Share Jumps to 68%(!) and Small BEVs Rise to Power — China EV Sales Report for October

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2010 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto 📈 Bullish 🌐 Cleantechnica ↗ Open Full Page

EV Share Jumps to 68%(!) and Small BEVs Rise to Power — China EV Sales Report for October

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2010 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • High gas prices and a never-ending wave of new BEVs have allowed October to reach 68% EV market share, a new record!
  • This record achievement is thanks to a significant ICE (internal combustion engine) crash.
  • Sources indicate that adding 45% BEV share to PHEVs (23% share) meant that in October a record 68% of all cars sold in China had a plug!
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

High gas prices and a never-ending wave of new BEVs have allowed October to reach 68% EV market share, a new record!

This record achievement is thanks to a significant ICE (internal combustion engine) crash. The overall market dropped 27% year over year (YoY), to around 1.6 million sales. Plugins were down 14% YoY, but pure ICE sales were much worse off, crashing 44% YoY!

Sources indicate that adding 45% BEV share to PHEVs (23% share) meant that in October a record 68% of all cars sold in China had a plug! If this trend continues in the future, the Chinese market will be fully electrified by 2030, and will be 100% BEV before 2035!

Recent findings suggest that this great result pulled the 2026 share up, to 59%, already 5% above the full year result of 2025. BEVs on their own were up to 40% (versus 33% in 2025).

Recent findings suggest that at this pace, I expect the final number for 2026 EV share in China to be above 60%, with BEVs alone north of the 40% mark. And when the largest global automotive market gets this electrified … then the ICE industry is in serious trouble.

The ICE extinction is also visible in the overall ranking. The overall top 10 was fully made by EVs. Again.

Looking at the best sellers in several size categories, the ICE extinction is also quite visible. Although, once again, the C-segment/compact category is the exception, with the only ICE representative showing up there — the Toyota RAV4, in 2nd, behind the leader Nevo Q05 and just ahead of the BYD Dolphin.

Having a quick look at the five size categories, the highlight is the B-segment/subcompact category, which is the hottest segment right now, with three of the top four top sellers in October belonging to this category.

Considering that 56% of the new SUVs rolled out this year were bigger than 5 meters/197 inches, there is a clear disconnect between what people want (small hatchbacks/crossovers) and what OEMs offer (large SUVs).

Another highlight is the fact that Xiaomi had a gold plus silver win in the full size category, with the BYD Great Tang closing out the podium while the midsize category podium was 100% BYD Group.

Here’s more info and commentary on October’s top selling electric models:.

A BYD Dolphin for BYD Seagull money ($10,000). This was Geely’s internal memo to describe the formula for the Geely Xingyuan when developing its star model. With an interesting name — Xingyuan translates as “wishing upon a star” — it seems that Geely had its wish granted. However, the Geely model will have a tough adversary soon, as the upcoming generation Seagull will land with only one goal — to steal the Xingyuan’s best seller status. But while the new Seagull didn’t land, the small Geely scored a record performance in October, with its 50,190 registrations representing a 14% increase YoY. Besides the new BYD Seagull, Geely’s hatchback now has to deal with Leapmotor’s B-segment contenders, the A10 and A05; the new-generation Wuling Bingo; Chery’s new QQ3; and let’s not forget about BYD’s Yuan Up, too.

BYD’s midsize SUV continues to transition into the fresh generation. Thanks to the ramp-up of the new Ultra body, BYD’s star player was 2nd, scoring 30,772 registrations. Sales were up by 6% compared to the same month last year. The new Ultra generation features lidar and 1,500 kW DC charging, and these two features aren’t even the most impressive aspects of the model! That would be the price. It starts at 152,000 yuan (or $22,000) with the 76 kWh battery, and it goes up to 180,000 yuan (or $26,000) with the 83 kWh battery. For comparison, the Tesla Model Y starts in China at 259,000 yuan ($38,250)…. Expect the Song to experience a second youth from here onwards, and while it is impossible to displace the Tesla Model Y from the runner-up spot, the last place on the podium is doable this year. And maybe higher up in 2027?

BYD’s small crossover continues to surprise, thanks to recently improved specs. BYD’s team player rose to 3rd in October, scoring 28,514 registrations, which was a 44% increase YoY and a new record score. Despite not being the most exciting vehicle to look at, or drive, the truth is that it is surfing the wave of small, affordable EVs better than most, scoring high in value for money with prices starting at $11,000 and higher end versions having BYD’s driver-assistance system. With small vehicles currently having a moment in China, expect the small crossover to show up in the top 5 more regularly.

It has been revealed that things continue to go well for the startup brand, with its new baby A10 now established as the star player in an already strong lineup. Thanks to 27,247 registrations, the small crossover managed another top 5 presence. The model has the usual value-for-money focus of the brand, and a low, low price of 66,000 yuan ($10,000). On top of that, however, the A10 offers something close to a distinct personality, as the design eschews the white product standard design of Leapmotor for something more personal, mostly thanks to the front and back lights and a floating roof effect. With B-segment BEVs now being the hottest category in China, Leapmotor is well prepared to benefit from the subcompact rising tide, thanks to the recent arrival of the A10 small crossover and its sibling, the A05 small hatchback. Talk about perfect timing….

According to recent reports, after the SU7 and YU7, Xiaomi has another success on its hands. This big fat SUV — or shall I say SUVs, as the lineup is broken down between the 7-seat N90 and the 5-seat N70 — scored 27,132 registrations in only its second month on the market, pulling it immediately into the overall top 5. Even with the number of competitors growing every passing day, Xiaomi’s new land yachts have been selling like hot cakes, while drying up sales of the competition. Proof of that, is the fact that there were only two full size models in October’s top 20, with the other being … the Xiaomi SU7.

Looking at the rest of the best seller table, there were a number of models hitting record scores, starting with the #8 Nevo Q05 (20,022 units) continuing its success story. The #10 Bestune Xiaoma (17,887 units) benefitted from a recent refresh to score a surprise record score. Could this mean that small city EVs are (finally) seeing the light at the end of the tunnel?

It has been revealed that as for the second half of the table, the highlight is the ramp-up of the Xpeng L03, with the attractive looking crossover, which kind of reminds of a mini-Lotus or small Polestar, reaching 13th thanks to 15,653 sales. This EV looks to be the startup’s star model thanks to a competitive price (124,000 RMB) that is half the price of the Tesla Model Y!

Other models with record performances were the #14 MG 4 (15,503 units), with the new generation proving to be much more popular and adaptable to local tastes than the previous one, and the #17 Chery QQ3 EV, which continued its slow climb in the ranking thanks to 14,041 sales, which made it the 5th B-segment model in the top 20.

Still in the top 20, we should also highlight the best selling foreign model, the Tesla Model Y VW ID.Aura T6, the latest China-made (and China-developed) German crossover that has allowed Volkswagen to beat the Texans for the first time in years (the Tesla Model Y was down 60% YoY, to 7,807 units, while the Model 3 was down 85%, to 1,010 units). The Aura T6, VW’s take on the Model Y formula, rose to the 20th position in its first full month on the market!

A promising sign, or just hype? Only time will tell, but at least for now, VW seems to be getting some traction on the EV side of the Chinese market, a point also highlighted by the fact that it wasn’t just the Aura T6 getting decent sales. The also new VW ID.Era 5S (think Chinese VW Jetta) got 7,100 registrations in October. Is there hope after all?

Outside the top 20, the main event was the ramp-up of Nevo’s fresh baby, the Q06, which is looking to replicate the Q05’s success in the category above. With some 10,000 registrations in only its second month, it looks like it could join the top 20 soon. The same can be said about the Geely Galaxy TT, the make’s answer to the Xiaomi SU7, which had around 10,500 deliveries in October. Then there’s also the BYD Yuan Plus, which, after a long cross through the desert, seems to be picking up steam again. It scored 11,658 registrations last month, a new year best.

Industry observers note that looking at the 2026 ranking, the podium remained the same, and unless something unexpected happens, it should stay as it is until the end of the year, with the small Geely repeating its 2025 win. That also means the Tesla Model Y will return to silver after getting bronze in 2025, and the BYD Song will get back onto the podium after a one-year absence.

Industry observers note that below the podium positions, though, there was some news. The BYD Yuan Up and Leapmotor A10 are surfing the B-segment wave and both climbed a position, to 5th and 6th, respectively.

If the BYD Yuan Up continues on its current record streak, then the small crossover could even aim to surpass the #4 FCB Ti7 before the year ends.

Still, with three subcompacts right now in the top 6 (Geely Xingyuan, BYD Yuan Up, and Leapmotor A10), small is hot right now, in China.

Elsewhere, the BYD Sealion 05 was up two positions, to 16th, while the Wuling Mini EV is hoping to bring tiny city cars back into the spotlight, and in October, it jumped two positions, ending the month in 13th….

Looking at the overall manufacturer ranking, it is a sea of red. Everyone is losing sales — major time. The exception is #5 Leapmotor (+31% YoY), while #8 Xiaomi (+3% YoY) and #10 Xpeng (+0%) are just hanging on.

So, now, not only are foreign OEMs suffering (Nissan was down 70% in October, Honda was down 51%), but even domestic ones are being affected by the EV shift.

Some may be asking, “But what about #9 Nevo and its 125% growth rate?” Well, it isn’t so much that they are winning sales, but they are effectively replacing the sales of their mother brand, Changan, which in October was only 19th after a 60% drop in sales YoY.

Looking at the auto brand ranking, BYD is firmly in the leadership position (17.2%), while runner-up Geely held to its 7.1% market share.

Rising 3rd placed Leapmotor (6.7%, up 0.2%) is fast approaching Geely. It wouldn’t be surprising if the startup brand became the new silver medalist in the final days of the year.

Sources indicate that one thing is for certain though — Leapmotor will win its first medal this year. The only question is the material that it will be made of….

Speaking of position changes, Tesla had a horrible month (4.4%, down from 4.9% in September), which allowed Wuling (4.6%) to climb one position in October, into 4th. At the end of the year, expect Tesla to keep the #4 position, as its December peak should help it surpass Wuling.

Looking at OEMs/automotive groups/alliances, BYD is leading with 21.9% share of the market, up 0.1% in October.

Sources indicate that meanwhile, Geely remained in second with 11.8% share. The multinational conglomerate has the runner-up spot secured.

Industry observers note that #3 SAIC was stable (8%) and remained firm in the last place on the podium, while #4 Leapmotor (6.7%, up 0.2%) remained on the rise. Will we see the startup challenge SAIC in 2027 for the 3rd spot?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The digital world has revolutionized how real estate is marketed and sold, placing a premium on strategic online presence and data-driven advertising. Among the myriad online tools available, Schema Markup stands out as an extremely potent weapon for real estate agents. This article offers a comprehensive look at how real estate agents can effectively use Schema Markup to bolster their online presence, increase organic reach, and drive sales.

Before discussing its application, let's first demystify what Schema Markup is. Schema Markup, also known as Structured Data, is a form of microdata. Once added to a webpage, it creates an enhanced description (commonly known as a rich snippet), which appears in search results. Developed by a collaborative team from Google, Yahoo!, Bing, and Yandex, Schema.org was debuted in 2011 to create and support a common set of schemas for structured data markup on web pages.

Recent findings suggest that to break it down simply, Schema Markup tells the search engine what your data means, not just what it claims. This enhanced understanding allows search engines to present more detailed and accurate snippets of your site to users, increasing click-through rates (CTR), boosting organic search rankings, and potentially improving conversion rates.

Why Real Estate Agents Need Schema Markup.

It has been revealed that schema Markup is incredibly beneficial to real estate professionals. The real estate industry is hyper-local, and search engine queries reflect this. Buyers and sellers are often searching with a specific location in mind. A real estate agent using Schema Markup can provide rich, location-based information directly in search results, making their listings more likely to be clicked on. It's an opportunity to outshine competitors and improve visibility in local search results.

Furthermore, Schema Markup helps real estate websites become more comprehensible to search engines. This enhanced understanding translates into more accurate categorization, increased visibility, and a better chance of appearing in relevant search results. In a landscape where digital prominence equates to business success, Schema Markup is no longer a luxury but a necessity for every real estate agent.

Implementing Schema Markup for Real Estate.

#87930. Every Car Brand That's Put Rotary Engines In Production Cars (There Aren't Many)

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1137 w)
📖 Baca

Every Car Brand That's Put Rotary Engines In Production Cars (There Aren't Many)

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1137 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that beyond the realms of car enthusiasm, most normies wouldn't have actually heard of a rotary engine – also known as a Wankel engine (after Felix Wankel, the man who patented the design in the first place).
  • In a recent development, when it comes to street cars, the most coveted example is Mazda's famous RX-7.
  • It has been revealed that but Mazda isn't the only car brand to have ever used a rotary engine in its production cars.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that beyond the realms of car enthusiasm, most normies wouldn't have actually heard of a rotary engine – also known as a Wankel engine (after Felix Wankel, the man who patented the design in the first place). These are fondly called "spinning Doritos" because at their heart is a triangular rotor that whizzes around a central shaft and makes power in a similar way to how a regular piston engine does. There are many pros and cons to rotary engines, and the cons are why they have seldom been used in automobiles.

In a recent development, when it comes to street cars, the most coveted example is Mazda's famous RX-7. The same brand was also responsible for arguably the most mythical race car ever created: the quad-rotor 787B. It won the 1991 edition of the famed 24 Hours of Le Mans and leaves a lasting impression on anyone who hears it, thanks to the orgasmic, high-pitched wail it generates as it climbs toward 9,000 rpm.

It has been revealed that but Mazda isn't the only car brand to have ever used a rotary engine in its production cars. The very first instance came from a German company called NSU (which eventually became part of Audi), and there were also examples from Citroën and the Russian brand Lada. Maxton, a low-volume sports car maker from the U.S., also briefly used rotary engines in the Rollerskate. But since it used Mazda engines and was built in such small numbers, it is often discounted.

In fact, the famed Japanese brand is estimated to have built around two million rotaries between 1967 and 2012, starting with the much-loved Cosmo sports car and ending with the equally adored RX-8 coupe. It has since resurrected the rotary, but only as a generator that forms part of a hybrid package in the MX-30 electric SUV, so it hardly counts.

Mazda really did try it all at the height of its rotary days, even building the now highly collectible Rotary Pickup. It was — and is — humanity's sole rotary-powered pickup truck, equipped with a 110-horsepower 1.3-liter Wankel unit, and made purely for the U.S. and Canadian markets. The company built around 15,000 examples, and well-maintained, low-mileage trucks still go for close to $30,000. Further afield, ardent enthusiasts will also remember the Mazda Furai concept, which is among the weirdest one-off cars ever built.

It has been revealed that before Mazda's love affair with Wankels, NSU rolled out the very first rotary-powered production car, the Spider, at the 1963 Frankfurt Auto Show. Its single-rotor, 500cc engine wasn't hugely powerful: it produced just 50 hp when it debuted, and maxed out at 54 hp in its most powerful guise. Despite getting positive reviews from the automotive press, the Spider never really took off. Just 2,400 units are estimated to have been built before production ended in 1967.

NSU replaced it with the Ro 80, which was a sleek, four-door sedan with a 115-hp twin-rotor motor and a fancy independent suspension. It was so good that European Car of the Year jurors voted it as their winning candidate for 1968 – making it the first German vehicle to ever win the coveted prize. It enjoyed a 10-year run rolling off the production lines, with NSU building around 37,000 examples before retiring it in 1977.

It was in 1964 that Citroën struck up a partnership with NSU to develop rotary engines. While NSU went on to join the VW Group, Citroën stayed the course and eventually unveiled the M35 in the late '60s — its first true rotary-powered car, built in a limited run of 267 examples. Based on an Ami 8 – the same model James May used during the "Top Gear" classic time trial rally challenge in Mallorca – the M35 even had Citroën's super-soft hydropneumatic suspension, with 49 rampant French horses under the hood.

Then came the GS Birotor in 1973, whose twin-rotor setup produced an even mightier 106 hp and allowed for a top speed of 109 mph. Citroën eventually dropped its rotary experiment by the late '70s, in part due to low sales volumes, but also because of the world's oil crisis. The latter is significant here because rotary engines, by nature, guzzle fuel. They burn a lot of oil, too.

Yes, who'd have thought it? Little about these cars ever made it past the Iron Curtain, but Lada started its Wankel journey in 1978 with the VAZ-21018. Though it may have shared model codes with a fax machine of some kind, the 21018 did have a pretty prominent place in society. The four-door sedan used a 71-hp rotary engine that was basically reverse-engineered from either an NSU or a Mazda engine, depending on who you ask, and proved horribly unreliable. Some accounts say these engines couldn't manage more than 12,000 miles before succumbing to issues such as seal and bearing failures.

Recent findings suggest that lada took another crack at it in 1982 and created a twin-rotor engine with two outputs: 115 and 140 hp. These were fitted to the VAZ-21019 sedan, and provided a notable step up in performance from "regular" Ladas. They proved slightly more reliable too, at the cost of poorer fuel economy. Lada did stick by its rotary engines all the way until the early 2000s, albeit on an increasingly small scale, before wrapping up production entirely.

Citroën, Mazda, Lada, and NSU aren't the only manufacturers to have dabbled with rotary cars. General Motors was at the height of its power in the '70s, and saw an opportunity to reinvent how vehicles were engineered by placing rotaries at the heart of its looks. It had intended to offer its then-latest Vega compact car with a Wankel engine, and committed $50 million just to license the technology. There was even the Aerovette: the best-looking Corvette of all time that never made it out of the concept stage and had a rotary engine. Unfortunately, as would soon happen with Citroën and the GS Birotor, the global oil crisis forced GM to ditch its rotary plans by the end of 1974.

Mercedes-Benz also got in on the act with its jaw-dropping C 111 experimental vehicle, first previewed at the 1969 Frankfurt Auto Show. It seemingly had everything a discerning celebrity would've wanted back then: a funky wedge-shaped body, a striking orange metallic paint job, and gullwing doors. Whereas the very first experiment had a three-rotor configuration, the second cranked it up to four rotors and was claimed to have a top speed of 186 mph. It all sounds super exciting, right? Well, Mercedes chose not to put it into production. Sorry to burst your several-second dream of owning one. But of the rotary-powered cars that did make production, which would you most like to own?

#87925. Breaking: Alzheimer’s may have early warning signs outside the brain

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1459 w)

General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Alzheimer’s may have early warning signs outside the brain

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1459 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Alzheimer's disease is best known for its effects on memory and thinking, but new research suggests that some symptoms may develop in a surprising place: outside the brain.
  • It has been revealed that scientists at the University of Central Florida (UCF) have discovered that genetic mutations associated with Alzheimer's can interfere with the nerves that control muscle movement, even without involvement from the brain or spinal cord.
  • The discovery raises the possibility that movement difficulties could provide earlier warning signs of the disease and that treatments focused exclusively on the brain may overlook crucial problems elsewhere in the body.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Alzheimer's disease is best known for its effects on memory and thinking, but new research suggests that some symptoms may develop in a surprising place: outside the brain.

It has been revealed that scientists at the University of Central Florida (UCF) have discovered that genetic mutations associated with Alzheimer's can interfere with the nerves that control muscle movement, even without involvement from the brain or spinal cord. The findings could help explain why some people with Alzheimer's experience changes in walking, balance, or coordination long before noticeable memory problems emerge.

The discovery raises the possibility that movement difficulties could provide earlier warning signs of the disease and that treatments focused exclusively on the brain may overlook crucial problems elsewhere in the body.

According to recent reports, the research was led by James Hickman, a professor at UCF's Nanoscience Technology Center, and Research Professor Xiufang "Nadine" Guo, working alongside scientists at the healthcare technology company Hesperos. Funded by the National Institutes of Health's National Institute on Aging, the study used laboratory systems built from human cells to investigate how inherited Alzheimer's mutations affect movement. The findings were published in Alzheimer's & Dementia: The Journal of the Alzheimer's Association.

It has been revealed that "Motor deficits may be an earlier indication [of Alzheimer's]," Guo says. "If we can detect those changes and intervene earlier, that could help delay the onset of central nervous system symptoms.".

Why Alzheimer's Symptoms May Appear Before Memory Loss.

Alzheimer's is generally associated with progressive memory loss, confusion, and declining cognitive abilities. However, doctors have also observed that some patients develop physical symptoms, including changes in balance, coordination, and gait (manner of walking), years before clear cognitive difficulties become apparent.

These observations have raised an vital question: Are such movement problems simply a consequence of damage occurring in the brain, or could Alzheimer's also interfere directly with nerves elsewhere in the body?

To investigate, the UCF team focused on familial Alzheimer's, a rare inherited form of the disease that typically develops earlier in life (from 40 to 65 years of age) than the more common form.

Their experiments revealed that motor neurons carrying mutations linked to familial Alzheimer's could disrupt the connections responsible for controlling muscles, even when the brain and spinal cord were completely absent from the experimental system.

Motor neurons are specialized nerve cells that transmit signals to muscles, telling them when to contract and produce movement. The newly introduced findings suggest that Alzheimer's mutations can interfere with this process directly, rather than affecting movement only through damage to the brain.

"This is the first time it's been demonstrated that deficits in the peripheral nervous system can arise directly from these mutations," Hickman claims. "It means drugs that target the brain may not fix problems in the rest of the body.".

The peripheral nervous system includes the nerves located outside the brain and spinal cord. These nerves carry signals between the central nervous system and the rest of the body, helping control movement, sensation, and other essential functions.

Recent findings suggest that guo also points out that preserving the ability to move could have benefits beyond physical health. Regular physical activity is associated with better cognitive well-being, so protecting motor function may also help support brain health.

How a Miniature Human Cell System Revealed the Discovery.

To examine the relationship between Alzheimer's mutations and muscle movement, the scientists used an innovative laboratory platform known as "human-on-a-chip" technology.

Developed and manufactured through Hesperos, a company co-founded by Hickman, these miniature systems bring different types of human cells together under controlled conditions. They allow researchers to recreate specific biological functions and observe how diseases interfere with them.

Recent findings suggest that unlike conventional laboratory experiments that examine isolated cells, these systems can reproduce notable interactions between different tissues. They also provide an alternative to animal models, which do not always accurately reflect how human diseases behave.

For this study, the team created a miniature model of the neuromuscular junction, the connection where a motor neuron communicates with a muscle cell.

The model was deliberately designed without a brain or spinal cord. This was a crucial part of the experiment because it allowed the researchers to investigate whether Alzheimer's-related changes could cause movement problems independently of the central nervous system.

Recent findings suggest that the scientists combined healthy muscle cells with motor neurons derived from stem cells that carried genetic mutations associated with familial Alzheimer's disease. Stem cells are cells that can develop into specialized types of cells, making them valuable tools for studying human diseases in the laboratory.

The researchers then examined how effectively the altered nerve cells communicated with otherwise healthy muscle tissue.

It has been revealed that the results showed that the Alzheimer's-associated mutations could interfere with normal nerve-to-muscle function. This suggests that at least some movement difficulties linked to the disease may arise directly in the peripheral nervous system rather than being caused entirely by degeneration in the brain.

Why Damaged Nerve Connections Can Affect Walking and Balance.

Every voluntary movement depends on successful communication between the nervous system and the muscles.

Recent findings suggest that at the neuromuscular junction, an electrical signal traveling along a motor neuron triggers chemical communication that causes a muscle to contract. This process makes everyday activities possible, from walking and maintaining posture to lifting objects and performing precise movements.

When the connection becomes impaired, muscles may respond less effectively to nerve signals. Depending on the severity and location of the problem, this can contribute to weakness, reduced coordination, and difficulty sustaining physical activity.

To evaluate these effects, the research team measured how consistently nerve signals produced muscle contractions and how long the muscles could continue contracting before becoming fatigued.

According to recent reports, these measurements provided a direct assessment of how well the nerve and muscle cells worked together. They also resemble aspects of the functional testing physicians use when examining patients with movement disorders.

"You can't move unless the motor circuit works," Hickman says. "When a doctor taps your knee to check your reflex, they're testing that exact connection.".

By demonstrating impaired nerve-to-muscle communication in a system containing no brain or spinal cord, the study provides evidence that mutations linked to familial Alzheimer's can produce effects beyond the central nervous system.

However, the experiments do not establish that these changes necessarily occur before memory loss in patients. Further research will be needed to determine how closely the laboratory findings reflect the progression of Alzheimer's in people, particularly those with the more common forms of the disease.

Could This Discovery Lead to Earlier Alzheimer's Detection?

The findings suggest a potentially key newly introduced direction for Alzheimer's research: looking beyond memory and other cognitive symptoms when investigating the disease.

If future studies confirm that changes in motor function are detectable early in certain patients, tests of walking, coordination, or nerve-to-muscle activity might eventually help identify disease-related changes before more obvious neurological symptoms develop.

In a recent development, the results also raise questions about treatment. Many Alzheimer's therapies are designed to address processes occurring in the brain, but medications that target the central nervous system may not necessarily correct abnormalities affecting peripheral nerves and muscles.

Understanding these separate effects could help researchers investigate treatments that protect physical function alongside cognitive health.

Human-on-a-Chip Technology Could Transform Disease Research.

Beyond the implications for Alzheimer's, the researchers see considerable potential in using human-on-a-chip systems to investigate other diseases and evaluate possible treatments.

Because these platforms contain human cells and reproduce measurable biological activities, they can help scientists observe disease-related changes in conditions that more closely resemble human physiology than some conventional experimental models.

This approach may be particularly useful in drug development, where researchers need to understand not only how a potential treatment affects individual cells but also how it influences interactions between different tissues.

Such systems can also uncover biological effects that may be difficult to detect in animal experiments, potentially helping researchers identify promising therapies and recognize limitations earlier in development.

For Hickman, the progress represents the culmination of three decades of work devoted to understanding disease through more realistic laboratory models.

"These systems let us study disease in a way that's closer to what actually happens in the human body, and that's what we need to develop better treatments," he states.

Latest Update: Obesity linked to up to 27% lower risk of death in dementia

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A surprising newly introduced study has found that people who are overweight or obese when diagnosed with dementia tend to live longer than those who have a normal body weight.
  • It has been revealed that researchers from Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health and NYU School of Global Public Health found that body weight at the time of diagnosis may provide key clues about how long someone with dementia is likely to live.
  • The results are particularly intriguing because obesity is well established as a risk factor for several serious health problems, including heart disease and diabetes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A surprising newly introduced study has found that people who are overweight or obese when diagnosed with dementia tend to live longer than those who have a normal body weight. The findings challenge expectations about the relationship between weight and health, suggesting that carrying extra weight may be associated with an unexpected survival advantage after dementia develops.

It has been revealed that researchers from Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health and NYU School of Global Public Health found that body weight at the time of diagnosis may provide key clues about how long someone with dementia is likely to live. Their findings, published in the Journal of Alzheimer's Disease, also highlight the importance of proper nutrition for people living with the condition.

The results are particularly intriguing because obesity is well established as a risk factor for several serious health problems, including heart disease and diabetes. Being overweight or obese during middle age is also associated with a greater likelihood of developing dementia later in life. However, previous research has suggested that the relationship may reverse once dementia has developed, with higher body weight linked to better survival.

According to recent reports, "Because this finding is somewhat counterintuitive, an notable question is whether it could simply be an artifact of bias. Our analyses suggest that the major sources of bias we examined do not explain the survival advantage associated with higher weight," stated corresponding author Yuan Zhang, PhD, assistant professor of Sociomedical Sciences at Columbia Mailman and in the Butler Columbia Aging Center.

Obesity Linked to Up to 27% Lower Risk of Death.

The researchers found substantial differences in survival based on body weight at the time of dementia diagnosis. Compared with individuals in the normal weight range, those who were overweight or obese had a significantly lower risk of death, even after the researchers accounted for smoking, existing medical conditions, and demographic characteristics.

Industry observers note that people classified as overweight (body mass index of 25 to 29.9) had a 16 percent lower risk of death. Those with class 1 obesity (BMI of 30 to 34.9) had an even larger reduction of 27 percent, while individuals with class 2 and 3 obesity (BMI equal to or greater than 35) had a 22 percent lower risk.

Despite these striking differences, the researchers caution that the findings should not be interpreted as a recommendation for people with dementia to gain weight.

"This doesn't mean that patients with dementia should attempt to become overweight or obese, as our study was not designed to test that question. But our findings do suggest that weight status may serve as a useful prognostic signal for survival at the time of dementia diagnosis. They also support the notion that nutrition is a key factor in the health and survival of people with dementia," remarked Virginia Chang, associate professor of Social and Behavioral Sciences at NYU School of Global Public Health and the study's first author.

Tracking Weight and Dementia Over 24 Years.

To investigate the connection, Zhang, Chang, and their colleagues examined information from the Health and Retirement Study, a nationally representative research project that follows Americans ages 51 and older.

The team analyzed records collected between 1998 and 2022, focusing on 4,523 participants who did not have dementia when they entered the study but subsequently developed the condition.

Recent findings suggest that because the data covered such a long period, the researchers could examine how participants' weight changed in the years leading up to their diagnosis. They could also determine their weight when dementia was identified and track their survival afterward.

Industry observers note that this extended timeline was especially important because scientists have questioned whether the apparent benefit of higher body weight is genuine or simply reflects misleading patterns in the data. One possibility is that having additional fat or muscle gives patients resources that help them withstand the physical effects of dementia. Another is that the association arises from factors that earlier studies did not adequately consider.

Could Weight Loss Explain the Dementia Paradox?

One major concern involves weight loss that occurs before dementia becomes clinically apparent.

Earlier research by Zhang and Chang found that people can begin losing weight as much as 10 years before a dementia diagnosis, with the decline becoming more pronounced as the disease approaches.

This creates a potential problem for studies that measure weight only at the time dementia is diagnosed. Some individuals classified as having a normal weight may previously have been heavier and lost weight because of the developing disease. If those individuals are already experiencing more advanced illness, they may face a greater risk of death, making higher body weight appear beneficial by comparison.

The researchers also considered other possible distortions. Restricting an analysis to people who develop dementia can create misleading relationships between obesity and mortality, even when the underlying connection is more complicated.

Recent findings suggest that another concern is known as "survivor" bias. Since people with obesity face an increased risk of dying from certain illnesses before reaching the age when dementia typically develops, those who survive long enough to receive a dementia diagnosis may represent an unusually healthy group.

To determine whether these factors explained the findings, the team performed additional analyses designed to evaluate several potential sources of bias. The results indicated that the biases they examined were unlikely to be major drivers of the observed connection between higher weight and lower mortality.

Why Extra Weight Might Help People With Dementia.

Although the precise explanation remains unknown, the researchers identified several biological reasons why additional body weight could be advantageous for someone already living with dementia.

One possibility involves the body's energy reserves. People with more stored fat or greater muscle mass may be better equipped to withstand periods of poor nutrition and the physical deterioration that can accompany the disease.

In a recent development, dementia can interfere with eating in several ways. Changes in brain function may reduce appetite or motivation to eat, while some patients experience increased energy needs or gradually lose the ability to feed themselves. Over time, these problems can contribute to significant weight loss, muscle wasting, and declining health.

"Nutrition can be a substantial problem for people with dementia," remarked Chang. "They may experience wasting and an inability to eat, which can be due to changes in the brain's central drive, leading to loss of appetite and initiative, increased energy expenditure, and difficulties feeding themselves.".

Having additional energy stores or muscle tissue could potentially help patients cope with these challenges, although the study did not establish that these factors directly explain the survival differences.

The researchers emphasize that important questions remain unanswered. Even after examining multiple potential biases and identifying plausible biological explanations, they cannot say for certain why overweight and obese participants experienced lower mortality.

Nevertheless, Zhang and Chang believe that weight at the time of a dementia diagnosis could provide valuable information about a patient's likely survival. The results also reinforce the importance of recognizing and addressing nutritional problems in people with dementia.

Additional study authors include Eleanor Hayes-Larson of the University of Southern California and Hui Zheng of the University of Toronto.

The research received funding from the National Institutes of Health (grant numbers R00AG070274, R00AG075317).

Resolve AI’s SRE-1 model finds root causes of production alerts as AI agents go on call

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Incident remediation company Resolve AI Inc.
  • Recent findings suggest that the new model, declared Wednesday, reflects the organization’s argument that while AI has transformed how software gets written, it has barely touched how software gets run.
  • SRE-1 is a 27 billion-parameter model built on open weights and trained by a team of 16 AI researchers over a final run of 7.4 days on up to 512 graphics processing units.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 18:11 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

Incident remediation company Resolve AI Inc. has announced the launch of SRE-1, a new model that has been trained to find the root cause of production alerts, and Primary On-call, a new service that puts its artificial intelligence agents on call ahead of human engineers.

Recent findings suggest that the new model, declared Wednesday, reflects the organization’s argument that while AI has transformed how software gets written, it has barely touched how software gets run. According to Resolve AI, production has no public training corpus to match the published code that models learned from, as incidents at each company stay private.

SRE-1 is a 27 billion-parameter model built on open weights and trained by a team of 16 AI researchers over a final run of 7.4 days on up to 512 graphics processing units. Measured on the same incidents before and after training, which used reinforcement learning alone, the pass rate for a single investigation rose from 6.9% to 38.8%.

Resolve AI used Snowflake Inc.’s Cortex Training, a serverless service for customizing open-weight models, to build SRE-1. Snowflake Senior Vice President of Engineering Vivek Raghunathan noted Resolve AI was the first design partner for the service.

In testing on 49 difficult live production cases, each run five times, an ensemble of five SRE-1 investigations matched the strongest frontier model tested at a lower cost, according to the company. Resolve AI also benchmarked its complete system on 178 production alert investigations, solving about twice as many incidents as general-purpose coding agents.

According to recent reports, primary On-call puts that research to work on the critical path. Each page is investigated across telemetry, infrastructure, code and operational knowledge, according to the tech giant. Depending on what it finds, the agent can close the alert, mitigate the problem where a team’s policies permit or escalate to a human. Once it has acted, the agent checks the fix against the production baseline, monitoring it until recovery holds.

It has been revealed that the agent also links related alerts and investigations into a shared view of each underlying problem. For teams wary of handing over the pager straight away, Resolve AI offers a shadow mode that records the call the agent would have made on each page.

Up to 80% of paged alerts in production are noted to be handled by Primary On-call without escalation. Customers have reported a tenfold improvement in mean time to resolution, along with root-cause accuracy of up to 95%, according to Resolve AI.

Recent findings suggest that salesforce Inc. is among the early consumers. Bhupesh Patel, a software engineering principal architect at Salesforce, said that in the first few weeks of dark launch testing, the agent closed more than 70% of the CRM Analytics team’s paging alerts “without waking an engineer.”.

“No engineering team can keep up with how fast code and patches land in production,” said Resolve AI Chief Executive Spiros Xanthos. “The answer is agents that are accurate and fast enough to sit on the critical path, and that takes a model built for production.”.

It has been revealed that primary On-call is now generally available. Access to SRE-1 is limited to Resolve AI’s own platform.

Resolve AI is a venture capital-backed startup that has raised more than $190 million to date, including a $40 million extension to its Series A round in April, led by DST Global and Salesforce Ventures, that valued the company at $1.5 billion. Notable customers include Coinbase Global Inc., DoorDash Inc., Figma Inc., MSCI Inc., Nasdaq Inc., SAP SE and Zscaler Inc.
