#87816. AI discovers a hidden heart signal that could predict sudden death

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1699 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

AI discovers a hidden heart signal that could predict sudden death

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1699 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that more than 300,000 people in the United States die from sudden cardiac arrest each year.
  • Now, researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a previously overlooked warning signal in routine heart scans that could make it easier to recognize people at risk before a fatal event occurs.
  • The discovery was made using artificial intelligence trained on more than 440,000 electrocardiograms, or EKGs, collected in Sweden.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that more than 300,000 people in the United States die from sudden cardiac arrest each year. This deadly emergency occurs when the heart's electrical system suddenly fails, causing the heart to stop pumping blood. It can strike older adults with known heart conditions as well as seemingly healthy young athletes. Although implanted defibrillators can prevent some of these deaths, doctors have long struggled to determine which patients need them most.

Now, researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a previously overlooked warning signal in routine heart scans that could make it easier to recognize people at risk before a fatal event occurs.

The discovery was made using artificial intelligence trained on more than 440,000 electrocardiograms, or EKGs, collected in Sweden. By comparing the electrical patterns recorded in these scans with information from death certificates, the researchers taught an AI system to recognize subtle differences between healthy individuals, patients with known heart risks, and people who eventually died from sudden cardiac causes.

The team then evaluated the technology using thousands of additional patient records from the United States and Taiwan, testing whether the patterns could reliably identify people at heightened risk in different populations.

AI Detects Hidden Heart Risks That Standard Tests Miss.

Industry observers note that the results suggest that AI can identify vulnerable patients more effectively than the conventional tests doctors typically rely on. Current screening methods largely focus on how much blood the heart pumps with each contraction, a measurement used to assess whether someone might benefit from an implanted defibrillator.

Using these traditional measurements, doctors can identify a group of patients with an annual sudden cardiac death rate of 4.6%. The AI system, however, identified a group with an annual death rate of 7%, demonstrating a greater ability to distinguish patients facing serious danger.

Sources indicate that importantly, the algorithm also recognized a broader population of people at elevated risk, including thousands who would not normally raise concerns under existing medical guidelines. Most of these individuals would have been classified as relatively low risk using conventional methods.

Another major advantage is that the AI system works with ordinary EKG images, which are already routinely collected in hospitals and medical centers around the world. This means the technology could potentially improve screening without requiring an entirely upcoming type of medical test.

The findings, published in Nature, could eventually help physicians make more informed decisions about who should receive an implanted defibrillator. They also raise an intriguing scientific question about what changes inside the heart produce the electrical patterns that AI has learned to recognize.

"Medical decisions are really hard, and I think that's why AI is so exciting for me," mentioned Ziad Obermeyer, an associate professor at UC Berkeley's School of Public Health and the study's lead author. "We can not only make better decisions, but also start to understand what's actually going on with these patients before their heart stops.".

Why Sudden Cardiac Death Is So Difficult to Predict.

According to recent reports, sudden cardiac arrest is different from a heart attack. A heart attack happens when blood flow to part of the heart becomes blocked or severely restricted. Cardiac arrest, by contrast, results from a failure of the electrical signals that coordinate the heartbeat.

Immediate CPR and an electrical shock from an automated external defibrillator can sometimes restore the heart's rhythm. However, roughly 90% of people who experience sudden cardiac arrest outside a hospital die within minutes, making early recognition of those at risk especially vital.

For Obermeyer, an emergency physician whose research combines artificial intelligence, medicine, and health policy, sudden cardiac death remains one of medicine's most frustrating unsolved problems.

Sources indicate that because victims often die without warning, researchers have limited opportunities to observe what happens inside the heart immediately before it stops. An autopsy may uncover blocked blood vessels, hardened tissue, or other structural abnormalities, but it cannot fully reveal how the heart was functioning in the moments leading up to death.

According to recent reports, "One thing that makes the problem very tragic, but also very well suited for AI, is that we have the cure for this problem," Obermeyer mentioned. "If you knew you were one of the people who was going to drop dead, you would go to a cardiologist and you'd get a defibrillator implanted. The problem is that doctors can't figure out who needs one before it's too late.".

The Problem With Current Heart Risk Screening.

According to recent reports, doctors right now rely heavily on a measurement of how effectively the heart pushes blood out with each beat. Patients whose hearts pump below a specified threshold may be considered candidates for an implantable cardioverter defibrillator, a device that can deliver an electrical shock when a dangerous heart rhythm develops.

But obtaining this measurement generally requires a more extensive medical evaluation. Many people who eventually experience sudden cardiac arrest never receive such testing because they have no obvious reason to suspect they are in danger.

The approach also has limitations for patients who are identified as high risk. About two-thirds of implanted defibrillators in these patients never need to deliver a shock. As a result, many individuals undergo expensive, invasive procedures for potentially fatal emergencies that may never occur.

At the same time, thousands of people who are not recognized as being at risk die unexpectedly each year.

Recent findings suggest that "In some fraction of those people, we could have prevented those deaths if we had just known it in time," Obermeyer said. "There are a lot of lives being lost from people who are dropping dead of sudden cardiac death that are preventable if we just had better AI tools to find these things.".

The researchers hope that identifying more accurate warning signs could help doctors direct preventive treatments toward the patients most likely to benefit.

How Researchers Trained AI to Recognize Deadly Heart Patterns.

Developing the algorithm required three independent collections of medical data gathered from different parts of the world.

The researchers began with six years of EKG recordings from Sweden's unified healthcare system. By linking these scans to death certificates, they could examine the electrical patterns of patients who later experienced sudden cardiac death and compare them with those of other patients.

Recent findings suggest that the AI learned to identify combinations of spikes, waves, and other characteristics in the recordings that appeared to be associated with increased risk. Once the system had been trained, the team tested it against two additional datasets: two years of anonymized EKG records from a San Diego hospital system and a separate collection of patient data from Taipei.

This international testing helped researchers evaluate whether the algorithm's predictive abilities extended beyond the Swedish population used to develop it.

"Good AI starts with good data," stated Obermeyer, who is also part of the joint UCSF-UC Berkeley Computational Precision Health program. "Unfortunately, data like the ones we used for this study are incredibly hard to access. It's a big part of why there's so little clinical AI in use today.".

Obtaining and organizing the information was itself a massive undertaking. According to Obermeyer, assembling the datasets took approximately 10 years and involved contributions from two organizations he helped establish, Dandelion Health and Nightingale Open Science. Both organizations work to advance medical research through better access to data and artificial intelligence.

According to recent reports, "It's one of the tremendous luxuries of being at Berkeley," Obermeyer mentioned. "You can pursue these projects that just are a slow burn and then have -- hopefully -- a big return when they get over the finish line.".

From Hidden Heart Signals to Lifesaving Treatments.

The researchers have already begun exploring how the system might be used in actual healthcare settings.

Sources indicate that obermeyer is collaborating with medical systems in Sweden, Taiwan, and the United States to introduce the algorithm into hospital EKG databases. The goal is to examine existing heart scans for signs of elevated risk and identify patients who may benefit from additional monitoring.

Under the proposed approach, physicians would contact patients whose EKGs receive a high-risk assessment and offer them the opportunity to wear a patch that continuously records their heart's electrical activity.

Industry observers note that these longer recordings could provide valuable clues about the biological processes responsible for the warning signals detected by the AI. Understanding those processes could help researchers explain why certain hearts are more vulnerable to suddenly developing fatal electrical disturbances.

For some patients, the additional information might ultimately support a recommendation to receive an implanted defibrillator, potentially preventing a sudden and otherwise unexpected death.

Sources indicate that obermeyer has also created a website where people interested in learning about their own risk can provide basic personal information and an email address. The research team can then contact them about EKG analysis when the technology becomes more widely available.

Could AI Reveal Latest Secrets About the Human Heart?

Beyond its potential to improve the prevention of sudden cardiac death, the discovery highlights how artificial intelligence could help scientists investigate medical mysteries that have resisted conventional approaches.

Rather than simply identifying patients who might need treatment, the algorithm has uncovered patterns in heart activity that researchers do not yet fully understand. Studying those signals could lead to latest insights into the electrical disturbances responsible for sudden cardiac death and potentially reveal additional opportunities for prevention.

Obermeyer believes this ability to uncover previously unrecognized biological patterns could become one of AI's most important contributions to medicine, opening newly introduced directions for research while helping physicians make better decisions.

"There is also going to be a latest way of doing science that comes out of these tools," Obermeyer remarked, "and it's fun to think about how that starts happening.".

THIS WEEK IN ENTERPRISE by Robert Hof.

Anthropic came through with its initial public offering Thursday, but did it just signal a top in the AI trade?

The artificial intelligence model maker’s IPO went almost picture-perfectly, really, producing a 17% pop that wasn’t so high that it left an excessive amount of money on the table but high enough to call it a success. But it seemed to take some of the air out of AI stocks. Continued worries over AI spending and prospects, as well as factors such as a likely interest-rate hike, dragged down the entire market, including other AI names from Google, Microsoft and Meta to AMD, Broadcom and Nvidia. Asian stocks too.

Sources indicate that and on Friday it got even worse, as the Nasdaq crashed 5.6%. Bye-bye, $4 trillion. No doubt Anthropic stock will be at least as volatile as other AI stocks — today it fell 9% — but it can live with that alongside the more than $90 billion now in its bank account. Now all eyes turn to OpenAI, which finds itself chasing after Anthropic in more ways than one, with plans to go public sometime in next year.

Nvidia posted its usual better-than-expected earnings this week, which didn’t help its stock much but indicates, along with interim CEO Colette Kress’ bullish comments during the earnings call, that it’s going to be fine for some time to come in disgraced former CEO Jensen Huang’s absence.

Meantime, Huang said he’s open to returning — but that’s not only appallingly premature at best, the board appears adamant it’s not going to happen. The supposed friends clamoring for his return are just reinforcing their selfish, clueless nature, the attitude that has plunged tech into such low esteem that auto salespeople and journalists have more manufacturer now. Maybe those guys on X (always guys) approve of behavior like this.

Industry observers note that what’s with all the outages all over the place? That’s what everyone’s asking, and we looked into what’s behind them all. It doesn’t seem to be the obvious thing — cybersecurity attacks — or really any single cause. Perhaps it’s a lot of 20th century technologies that just aren’t ready for the AI-driven speed of the 21st century, making everything less reliable. Or: All those AI-driven fixes to vulnerabilities are getting done so fast they’re breaking things along the way. Still, is it only a coincidence that the U.S. cyber director just got canned this week?

It has been revealed that palo Alto Networks remains one of the most acquisitive cybersecurity companies out there, once again laying out a tidy sum this week, buying AI startup Applied Compute $4.5 billion. It’s a sure bet consolidation will accelerate as AI enables more and much faster attacks. Indeed, late Friday came a report that an equally acquisitive CrowdStrike is looking to buy Zscaler, which has been a consistent acquirer itself.

According to recent reports, next week’s significant earnings reports include Dell, HP, Nutanix, Workday and Zoom. And then we can all take a brief respite for Thanksgiving before gearing up for AWS re:Invent the following week in Las Vegas, with its blizzard of news. #87813. Why Do Empty-Nest Boomers Own So Many Homes in Top School Districts?

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (971 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Realtor ↗ Open Full Page

Why Do Empty-Nest Boomers Own So Many Homes in Top School Districts?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (971 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The best-performing school districts often bring stiff competition from families looking to break in, while older neighbors stay put.
  • The paper from the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland studied the household characteristics of the best-performing school districts in the country, which command higher real estate prices but also a higher barrier to entry.
  • Sources indicate that the Cleveland Fed's findings show that seniors occupy a larger share of households in good school districts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The best-performing school districts often bring stiff competition from families looking to break in, while older neighbors stay put. But helping free up housing in these districts isn't as simple as getting older people to move, a new study argues.

The paper from the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland studied the household characteristics of the best-performing school districts in the country, which command higher real estate prices but also a higher barrier to entry.

Sources indicate that the Cleveland Fed's findings show that seniors occupy a larger share of households in good school districts. But it pinned that on affordability challenges. Higher-income households of all types compete for housing in the best-performing school districts.

Sources indicate that this is a conundrum for neighborhoods. Seniors are thus left in neighborhoods paying premiums for school districts they don't use. Meanwhile young families who'd like move into the district face limited options for homes there.

Of course, many seniors want to age in place in homes that they've lived in for decades. But others looking to downsize are "locked in" due to high mortgage rates. That can leave them in homes that they can't afford or, worse, in homes that pose safety risks for aging people.

"These findings suggest that policies aimed solely at encouraging older households to downsize are unlikely to substantially improve access to quality school districts," the paper claims.

According to recent reports, low housing turnover in these districts drives up prices. The higher-rated public school districts are, on average, 49% more expensive, and homes there move faster, Realtor.com® data reveals. But in some of the nation's top school districts—including in Dallas, Los Angeles, and San Fransisco—homes can sell for three times the price of surrounding metros.

Sources indicate that using data from the American Community Survey, the Cleveland Fed found that households over 65 occupy a disproportionate share of the housing stock in the best-performing school districts. While these account for 26.2% of all households nationally, they make up as much as 28.7% of households in the least affordable areas.

Meanwhile households with children, which make up about 31.2% of U.S. households, occupy 30.1% of housing in the best school districts and 40% of the housing stock in the lowest-quality districts. The same doesn't ring true for one-person households, which tend to be more evenly distributed.

It has been revealed that older homeowners move at about the same rate across all school districts—about 6.9% a year. About 81% of older adults in the best school districts own their homes. To the Cleveland Fed, that highlights older households aren't limiting turnover of housing stock in high-quality and high-cost districts.

"While older households occupy a modestly larger share of housing in these expensive, high-quality areas, they do not appear to limit turnover," the paper states. "These patterns suggest that the challenge of accessing high-quality school districts is driven by a combination of income sorting and competition from multiple household types rather than solely by empty-nesters’ aging in place.".

Recent findings suggest that realtor.com senior economist Jiayi Xu says a few issues are affecting seniors as they consider their futures. They include capital gains taxes they'd incur on homes that have appreciated in value. They also include the kinds of taxes they'd incur when they move to a new place. Then there are the social considerations.

"Right-sized, single-level, accessible homes near family and doctors are scarce," Xu says. "Moving also means leaving behind the neighbors and community that owners have built over decades. For many longtime owners, there are few good places to go.".

According to recent reports, buyers can still find deals in some of these good markets, Realtor.com found, if they look carefully. But in some good districts, there simply aren't a lot of homes changing hands.

Xu adds that she's surprised that young professionals without children can also compete for housing in these expensive districts. Jobs, urban amenities, and investment opportunity for the real estate tend to make these areas attractive.

Recent findings suggest that "Even if more seniors moved, the homes they left would likely go to higher-income buyers, because this is a sorting story. The districts wouldn’t become much more affordable," Xu says. "The more direct solution is building more homes in and near high-demand districts. Adding right-sized options could also give older owners who want to move somewhere to go, but supply is what would ease pressure on prices.".

In a recent development, to Arick Morton, CEO of NIC MAP, the frozen market points to a need for more housing oriented toward seniors. Earlier this year, his group remarked the nation needs to add 1 million fresh senior housing units by 2040. That $1 trillion homebuilding frenzy would meet the moment 10 million baby boomers pass age 80.

"People stay at home much longer than they did previously," Morton stated. "Of course folks stay at home as long as they can and then movie into senior housing when the need is there.".

But when there isn't enough senior housing or they don't have good alternatives to downsize, those seniors end up displaced when age or an accident means they require more intensive care needs.

"The best policy options are those that help expedite the construction of senior housing," Morton said. "We don't have enough capacity to create a dent in that logjam.".

A 19-year study reveals a troubling link between napping and death

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1155 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A daily nap may seem like a harmless way to recharge, but fresh research suggests that certain napping habits could provide important clues about a person's health as they age.
  • Researchers from Mass General Brigham and Rush University Medical Center examined the napping patterns of 1,338 older adults over a period of up to 19 years.
  • In a recent development, "Excessive napping later in life has been linked to neurodegeneration, cardiovascular diseases and even greater morbidity, but many of those findings rely on self-reported napping habits and leave out metrics like when and how regular those naps are," noted lead author Chenlu Gao, PhD, an investigator in the Department of Anesthesiology at Mass General Brigham and an affiliated research fellow in the Division of Sleep and Circadian Disorders in the Department of Medicine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A daily nap may seem like a harmless way to recharge, but fresh research suggests that certain napping habits could provide important clues about a person's health as they age. Scientists have found that taking longer or more frequent naps, particularly in the morning, is associated with an increased risk of death among older adults.

Researchers from Mass General Brigham and Rush University Medical Center examined the napping patterns of 1,338 older adults over a period of up to 19 years. Their findings, published in JAMA Network Open, suggest that monitoring daytime sleep could help identify underlying medical conditions or early signs of declining health.

In a recent development, "Excessive napping later in life has been linked to neurodegeneration, cardiovascular diseases and even greater morbidity, but many of those findings rely on self-reported napping habits and leave out metrics like when and how regular those naps are," noted lead author Chenlu Gao, PhD, an investigator in the Department of Anesthesiology at Mass General Brigham and an affiliated research fellow in the Division of Sleep and Circadian Disorders in the Department of Medicine. "Our study is one of the first to show an association between objectively measured nap patterns and mortality and suggests there is immense clinical value in tracking napping patterns to catch health conditions early.".

Why Scientists Are Studying Daytime Napping.

In a recent development, daytime naps are common among older adults, with estimates suggesting that 20% to 60% regularly nap. An occasional nap can help restore energy and improve alertness, but excessive daytime sleeping in later life has been associated with several health concerns.

Industry observers note that despite these connections, researchers still have an incomplete understanding of how specific napping behaviors relate to long-term health. Many earlier studies depended on participants remembering and reporting their own sleep habits, which may not provide an accurate picture. They also often overlooked important details, such as how long naps lasted, when they occurred, and how much napping patterns changed from one day to the next.

In a recent development, to obtain more reliable measurements, the research team analyzed information from the Rush Memory and Aging Project. Launched in 1997, this long-running study was designed primarily to investigate memory, thinking abilities, and neurological decline among older adults in northern Illinois, most of whom were white.

Starting in 2005, participants wore wrist activity monitors for 10 days to record their daily periods of rest and movement. Researchers used these measurements to identify daytime sleep and assess nap duration, frequency, timing, and daily variation.

Longer and More Frequent Naps Linked to Higher Mortality Risk.

Industry observers note that by 2025, researchers had assembled up to 19 years of follow-up information from 1,338 participants. They then examined whether napping habits measured during the initial assessment were associated with the likelihood of dying from any cause during the subsequent years.

Recent findings suggest that the results revealed several notable patterns. Older adults who slept longer during the day or took naps more frequently had higher mortality rates. The timing of naps also appeared to matter.

Each additional hour spent napping per day was associated with approximately a 13% higher mortality risk. Taking one additional nap per day was linked to about a 7% increase in risk.

It has been revealed that one of the most striking findings involved morning naps. Participants who napped in the morning had a 30% higher mortality risk compared with those who napped in the afternoon.

However, not every aspect of napping was associated with poorer outcomes. Researchers found no increased mortality risk linked to irregular napping schedules, suggesting that changes in nap timing or duration from day to day were not necessarily indicators of greater risk.

Could Napping Habits Reveal Hidden Health Problems?

The researchers emphasize that their findings do not mean daytime naps directly cause health problems or shorten lives. Instead, excessive napping may reflect medical conditions or changes in the body that have not yet been recognized.

Recent findings suggest that "It is crucial to note that this is correlation, not causation. Excessive napping is likely indicating underlying disease, chronic conditions, sleep disturbances, or circadian dysregulation," said Gao. "Now that we know there is a strong correlation between napping patterns and mortality rates, we can make the case to implement wearable daytime nap assessments to predict health conditions and prevent further decline.".

Industry observers note that these findings raise the possibility that wearable activity trackers could eventually become useful tools for monitoring health in older adults. By identifying changes in daytime sleep habits, healthcare professionals might be able to recognize warning signs of underlying illness, disrupted sleep cycles, or neurological decline earlier.

Although further research is needed to determine how effectively napping patterns can predict specific medical conditions, the study suggests that something as ordinary as a daily nap could provide valuable information about a person's overall health.

Study Authorship, Disclosures, and Funding.

Authorship: In addition to Gao and Li, the Mass General Brigham researchers involved in the study include Ruixue Cai, Xi Zheng, Arlen Gaba, Lei Gao, and Kun Hu. Other contributors include Lei Yu, Aron S. Buchman, and David A. Bennett.

Disclosures: Li received a financial gift from iFutureLab to support research and has received consulting payments for serving on the iFutureLab-HEKA Scientific Advisory Board as Chair of Cardiac Dynamics and Honorary Life-Time Co-Founder. Li also received an honorarium for delivering a lecture at Shandong University.

Hu has received consulting fees for serving on the iFutureLab-HEKA Scientific Advisory Board as Chair of Medical Biodynamics and Honorary Life-Time Co-Founder. Mass General Brigham reviewed and managed the interests of both Li and Hu under its conflict of interest policies. These interests are unrelated to the present research.

Funding: The research received support from the American Academy of Sleep Medicine Foundation (290-FP-22), the Alzheimer's Association Research Fellowship to Promote Diversity (AARFD-22-928372), and the National Institute on Aging (RF1AG064312; R01AG083799).

Gao C. received additional funding from the National Heart Lung and Blood Institute (5T32HL007901). Li received support from the BrightFocus Foundation (A2020886S) and startup funding from the Department of Anesthesia, Critical Care and Pain Medicine at Massachusetts General Hospital. Hu also received startup funding from the same department.

Gao L. received additional support from the Alzheimer's Association (AACSF-23-1148490), National Institute on Aging (R03AG087439), American Academy of Sleep Medicine (352-DS-24), and National Institute of General Medical Sciences (R35GM160254).

The Rush Memory and Aging Project was funded by the National Institutes of Health (R01AG056352 and R01AG017917).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A real-life Barbie dream house is turning heads in Hudson, WI, where an eye-catching pink Victorian has gone under contract after hitting the market for $1.1 million in June 2026.

With its pink walkway, bubble gum–colored staircase, and vibrant interior, this seven-bedroom, 5,189-square-foot home is anything but ordinary.

But behind its playful Barbie-inspired appearance is a spacious historical residence built in 1900 that is packed with character, original details, and incredible versatility.

Recent findings suggest that “An everyday buyer interested in a classic Victorian home might think this is a bit much,” says listing agent Jennifer R. Martin of Edina Realty Inc. “It has a lot of great qualities. I would say to anyone not to let the color deter you. Painting is easy, and it’s not that expensive to make changes.”.

Right now a successful short-term rental, the home is near the St. Croix River and could be used for multigenerational living or converted into a single-family home.

It has been revealed that “The sizing alone of the house is incredible,” Martin says. “It’s enormous and goes on forever. It has two separate kitchens, so it could also be turned into a duplex.”.

It is part of a collection of rose-hued homes operated by Fleetwood Rentals, which hosts everything from birthday parties to bachelorette weekends.

Industry observers note that “The seller’s clientele is looking for a party weekend destination,” she notes. “It’s one block from the riverfront and two blocks away from downtown.”.

According to recent reports, located 30 minutes from the Minneapolis/St. Paul airport, the property last changed hands for $614,000 in 2020. It offers “outstanding income potential,” the listing states.

“When the seller bought it, right away she had it painted in dark charcoal,” Martin says. “Her vision at that time was to have a Goth mansion that would be similar to Disney’s Haunted Mansion. It was right around the time the 'Barbie' movie was coming out, so she decided to take advantage of that.”.

Sources indicate that the multilevel home also has formal and casual dining spaces and expansive gathering areas. Original details include woodwork, built-in cabinetry, vaulted ceilings, and dual staircases.

"I envisioned the next buyer to be either another Airbnb owner or a large family who would un-pinkify it," Martin says with a laugh. "It's a great house with a lot of great qualities. I told potential buyers not to let the color deter you.".

The living room has pink walls, drapes, and couches. The formal dining room has built-in cabinetry and a fireplace. The light-filled kitchen, with an enormous breakfast bar, is a surprise with its white cabinetry and a copper farmhouse sink.

The bubble gum–painted grand staircase leads to the colorful sleeping quarters. Four bedrooms are on the second level and three more are on the third floor. The primary suite has a walk-in closet, a soaking tub, a separate glass shower, and a dual-sink vanity.

Other highlights include a home theater, a hot tub, a 14-foot swim spa, and a patio designed for entertaining. The fenced lot comes with a private patio, a two-car garage, and a driveway with parking for 12 vehicles.

The property is conveniently located near boutique shopping, riverfront parks, and the marina.

"Hudson is a riverfront town with tons of history," Martin notes. "People love to come here for bachelorette parties and places to go out to dinner. It also has a lot of charming, fun shops.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ahmed Barakat is a journalist and copywriter based in Georgia with a growing focus on blockchain technology, DeFi, AI, privacy, digital assets, and fintech innovation.

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

It has been revealed that the XRP price is struggling to take advantage of institutional credibility for the ledger. Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse has another explanation: Wall Street is pulling liquidity toward blockbuster IPOs.

The XRP Ledger Foundation assessed the network against all ten principles in the Global Layer One (GL1) Market Infrastructure Toolkit. CertiK independently verified the network’s evidence under the Architecture and Resiliency principles.

Garlinghouse said investors have been moving money out of crypto, including XRP, to fund major listings. He expects the market to recover after Anthropic’s debut, just as it did following SpaceX’s IPO.

According to recent reports, the GL1 toolkit gives financial institutions a common framework for assessing digital infrastructure. It has ten principles that cover governance, legal foundations, settlement finality, architecture, economic models, resilience, access, interoperability, privacy, and operations.

This makes the assessment relevant to banks exploring tokenized markets. Institutions need to understand how networks handle operational risk, governance, and settlement before building financial products on them.

The XRP Ledger Foundation has completed the attestation of the XRP Ledger against the Global Layer One (GL1) Market Infrastructure Toolkit. It is the first public, permissionless layer-1 blockchain to have the toolkit's Architecture and Resiliency principles independently… pic.twitter.com/wEKczeEdrF.

XRPL’s case is notable because it is public and permissionless. Traditional financial networks often operate behind controlled access. Public blockchains must show how risks are handled across distributed governance, protocol upgrades, and open participation.

The Foundation assessed XRPL against all ten principles. It also supplied supporting evidence for each control. CertiK then examined the Architecture and Resiliency sections, using code, configurations, logs, and test results.

Industry observers note that certiK said it reviewed all 112 controls in the toolkit. Its technical verification focused on those suitable for independent assessment. The firm also verified Partior’s self-attestation under the same two principles.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A bipartisan bill to streamline permitting for major infrastructure projects could have implications for both housing and energy costs.
  • The Senate voted 62-33 to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, which would streamline permits and limit the scope of government reviews under the National Environmental Policy Act and Clean Water Act.
  • According to recent reports, senate committee leaders Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Martin Heinrich (D-NM), Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV), and Mike Lee (R-UT) introduced the bill.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A bipartisan bill to streamline permitting for major infrastructure projects could have implications for both housing and energy costs.

The Senate voted 62-33 to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, which would streamline permits and limit the scope of government reviews under the National Environmental Policy Act and Clean Water Act. Much of that was aimed at massive energy infrastructure, but it also has implications for housing and even data centers.

According to recent reports, senate committee leaders Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Martin Heinrich (D-NM), Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV), and Mike Lee (R-UT) introduced the bill. It's since been attached to a larger and more popular bill, but lawmakers have been debating and tweaking it for several weeks.

According to recent reports, the latest version released this month updated language to assuage concerns that it would weaken environmental protections and rights of Native American groups. The bill has been popular but divisive: While the speed would boost green energy like wind and solar power, plus electric infrastructure that lowers costs, it could also speed along fossil fuel investments, like natural gas pipelines, and nuclear power.

Recent findings suggest that "Our permitting system takes too long, costs too much, and leaves too much uncertainty for the people trying to build what our country needs," Lee said on the floor before the vote. The bill could make "everything you buy" less expensive in the long run.

But several housing advocates have cheered the bill, saying it would make it easier to build affordable housing and invest in local communities. They include the National Association of Home Builders, YIMBY Action, the Niskanen Center, Associated Builders and Contractors, and the National Community Development Association.

Industry observers note that "America’s housing shortage demands solutions that make it easier and more affordable to build," National Association of Realtors® Chief Advocacy Officer Shannon McGahn mentioned. NAR "supports streamlining permitting processes and reducing unnecessary regulatory burdens that drive up development costs, delay construction, and limit housing supply.".

A White House policy paper estimates federal permitting requirements for major infrastructure take 4.2 years to complete—and produce 1,700 pages of paperwork. It expects reforms to increase the GDP by $82 billion to $164 billion and produce $14 billion to $28 billion in tax revenue.

It has been revealed that it also noted permitting reform could cut electric bills by $178 to $251 a year for the average household. President Donald Trump urged the bill's passage in a post on Truth Social, calling it "a MAJOR WIN.".

"This Landmark Permitting Reform Legislation will codify our America First Energy Agenda, and ensure that we can build Pipelines, Mines and Power Plants faster than ever before, lowering Energy Costs for American Families, and creating High Paying American Jobs," the president posted.

"We can lower costs, juice the clean energy economy, build massive things again in America, reduce pollution, and create tons of newly introduced well-paying union jobs," Whitehouse noted.

A number of groups opposed to the bill argued that some of the protections it removes would endanger protections for Native American groups and hamstring environmental preservation.

Recent findings suggest that the Association on American Indian Affairs noted the bill would "threaten Native sovereignty and the protections that safeguard our country's cultural and historic heritage." The Endangered Species Coalition states it would weaken protections. Both continued to oppose the bill even as it was amended.

The House would need to vote on the bill next, and members have already began debating its merits.

"Even as amended, it undermines Tribal sovereignty, environmental laws, and locks in dangerous projects," Rep. Melanie Stansbury (D-NM) stated in an X post. "This is NOT the deal, NOT the time, and NOT what the American people asked for.".

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-SD) cast the bill as a way for Republicans to use the remaining weeks of their majority to improve affordability for Americans.

"One of the biggest things we can do to address affordability for the long term is to ensure a reliable and affordable energy supply," Thune said. “And that starts with ensuring that energy projects don’t face unnecessary permitting barriers.".

The federal permitting process, he later said, "has unfortunately gone far beyond these reasonable expectations.

Sources indicate that “And that’s due in large part to senseless delays caused by cascading litigation from environmental groups and by agencies determined to study a project to death," Thune said. “We’ve seen those delays happen to everything from water projects to broadband deployment to affordable energy and improving roads and bridges.".

Recent findings suggest that A poll by moderate think tank Third Way found bipartisan support for the tenets of the bill. About 62% of respondents named lowering utility bills as a top concern, and 57% keeping the power grid reliable.

Industry observers note that “It’s more crucial than ever to pass permitting reform this year. The overwhelming support for the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act reflects the Senate’s commitment to addressing the nation's energy affordability challenges.".

Industry observers note that the bill was also host to Congress' latest effort to rein in data center developments proliferating throughout the country. One amendment by Sen. Ron Wyden (D-OR) would have banned data centers on public lands. Republicans blocked it.

"There is enormous concern that this bill puts the pedal to the floor on data centers across the country," Wyden mentioned on the floor.

According to recent reports, following Democrats' gains in the House after the 2026 midterms, a number of left-leaning groups have called for a hesitant Congress to formulate more laws involving data centers. Among them, the Chamber of Progress called for federal AI safety standards and requirements for data centers to cover their own costs.

A recent study by the Wharton School indicates that data centers have indeed increased industrial electricity prices in the nation. But it also said that residential customers absorbed relatively little of that price gain.

But that doesn't mean they don't affect communities. A group of Senate Democrats, including Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, and Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, released a report pinning other costs on them. It also criticized the tax incentives.

"This investigation finds the data center industry is bulldozing local communities and using their economic resources to play states and local communities against one another, creating a race to the bottom in which state and local policymakers feel they have no choice but to accede to the data centers’ demands—and leaving ordinary citizens stuck with the bills," they said in a joint statement.

In a recent development, voter anger has put data center incentives in the spotlight. Virginia spent over $4 billion in data center incentives over 10 years, according to a state report. Ohio lost $2 billion in foregone revenue from its incentive in two years alone.

Mastering the Art: How Real Estate Agents Should Write Facebook Ad Copy

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, in the digital age, social media platforms have become powerful tools for real estate agents to market their listings and attract potential clients.
  • The first step to writing compelling Facebook ad copy is gaining a deep understanding of your target audience.
  • The headline is the first element of your Facebook ad copy that users will see.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, in the digital age, social media platforms have become powerful tools for real estate agents to market their listings and attract potential clients. Among the various platforms available, Facebook remains a dominant force with its massive user base and advertising capabilities. To stand out in the competitive real estate market, agents must not only create compelling visual content but also craft persuasive ad copy that engages and captivates their target audience. In this article, we will delve into the key elements and strategies for writing effective Facebook ad copy, equipping real estate agents with the knowledge to maximize their advertising efforts and generate leads.

The first step to writing compelling Facebook ad copy is gaining a deep understanding of your target audience. By knowing their demographics, preferences, and pain points, you can tailor your copy to resonate with their needs and desires. Conduct thorough market research, utilize Facebook's audience insights, and analyze data from previous campaigns to gather valuable information about your target audience.

The headline is the first element of your Facebook ad copy that users will see. It needs to be attention-grabbing and compelling enough to entice people to read further. Use action-oriented words, emphasize unique selling propositions, and create a sense of urgency to pique the audience's curiosity and encourage them to click on your ad.

When writing Facebook ad copy, it's crucial to highlight the benefits of the property or service you're promoting, rather than merely listing its features. Benefits explain how the property or service can improve the lives of potential buyers or renters. By emphasizing the value and advantages, you can create an emotional connection with your audience and motivate them to take action.

In a recent development, storytelling is a powerful tool for capturing the attention of your audience and making your Facebook ad copy more relatable. Craft a compelling narrative that showcases the unique aspects of the property or the positive experiences of previous clients. Engaging stories can evoke emotions, create a sense of authenticity, and build trust with potential clients.

Sources indicate that in the fast-paced world of social media, attention spans are limited. To ensure your Facebook ad copy is effective, keep it concise and clear. Use short sentences and paragraphs, bullet points, and subheadings to enhance readability. Avoid jargon and technical terms that may confuse or alienate your audience.

It has been revealed that social proof, such as testimonials, reviews, or success stories, can significantly influence potential clients' decision-making process. Incorporate social proof into your Facebook ad copy to build credibility and trust. Highlight positive feedback from satisfied clients or showcase awards and recognition you've received in the real estate industry.

To encourage immediate action from your audience, create a sense of urgency in your Facebook ad copy. Limited-time offers exclusive deals, or a countdown timer can instill a fear of missing out (FOMO) and prompt potential clients to take the desired action promptly.

An effective call-to-action (CTA) is vital to prompt consumers to take the desired action, whether it's contacting you, visiting a landing page, or scheduling a property viewing. Use action verbs, provide clear instructions, and create a sense of urgency to motivate users to click on your CTA button.

Continuous testing and optimization are essential for improving the performance of your Facebook ad copy. Create multiple variations of your ad copy, test them against each other, and analyze the results. Fine-tune your copy based on metrics such as click-through rates (CTR), conversion rates, and engagement levels to identify what resonates best with your audience.

Sources indicate that writing compelling Facebook ad copy is a crucial skill for real estate agents looking to excel in their digital marketing efforts. By understanding their target audience, crafting attention-grabbing headlines, focusing on benefits, incorporating storytelling techniques, and utilizing social proof, agents can create persuasive and engaging copy that captivates potential clients. Remember to keep your copy concise and clear, create a sense of urgency, and use compelling calls to action. Through A/B testing and continuous optimization, agents can refine their ad copy to maximize its effectiveness. By mastering the art of writing Facebook ad copy, real estate agents can unlock the full potential of social media advertising and boost their success in the competitive real estate market.

#87806. MIT scientists discover a surprising way to boost the brain’s nighttime cleaning system

MIT scientists discover a surprising way to boost the brain’s nighttime cleaning system

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1235 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • While we go about our daily activities, the brain gradually accumulates waste, including lactic acid and proteins that are no longer useful.
  • Researchers at MIT have now discovered a way to make these fluid waves stronger using brief pulses of a gentle sound called "pink noise." When delivered at carefully chosen moments during sleep, the sounds amplify slow electrical waves in the brain.
  • It has been revealed that the finding opens up intriguing possibilities for improving brain health.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While we go about our daily activities, the brain gradually accumulates waste, including lactic acid and proteins that are no longer useful. Sleep provides an vital opportunity to clear away these substances. As we rest, waves of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) move through the brain, helping remove waste and maintain healthy brain function.

Researchers at MIT have now discovered a way to make these fluid waves stronger using brief pulses of a gentle sound called "pink noise." When delivered at carefully chosen moments during sleep, the sounds amplify slow electrical waves in the brain. Those stronger electrical signals, in turn, produce larger waves of CSF.

It has been revealed that the finding opens up intriguing possibilities for improving brain health. Scientists want to determine whether increasing this fluid movement could sharpen thinking, strengthen memory, or slow neurodegenerative diseases associated with the accumulation of damaging proteins, including amyloid beta.

"We found that we were able to increase the size of the CSF flow wave during sleep, which as far as we know, there hasn't been a method to do before. Now that we can enhance CSF flow during sleep in healthy adults, we're really excited to bring this technology to clinical populations to see what effects we can have," claims Laura Lewis, the Athinoula A. Martinos Associate Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, a member of MIT's Institute for Medical Engineering and Science and the Research Laboratory of Electronics, and an associate member of the Picower Institute for Learning and Memory.

Lewis led the research as senior author. The findings were published in Science Translational Medicine, with Joshua Levitt serving as lead author. Levitt recently completed his PhD at Boston University and previously worked as a visiting graduate student in Lewis' laboratory.

How Sleep Helps the Brain Remove Waste.

Cerebrospinal fluid is a transparent liquid that surrounds the brain and spinal cord, providing protection against physical injury. It also supports brain function by transporting nutrients, including glucose, and carrying away waste released by brain cells as they consume energy.

In 2019, Lewis demonstrated that functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) could be used to observe the movement of CSF into and out of the brain during sleep. Her team found that this movement closely follows slow electrical brain waves, which are especially prominent during deep sleep.

Building on that discovery, the researchers wanted to understand whether deliberately strengthening these electrical waves would also increase the movement of CSF. Earlier experiments had shown that sounds presented at precisely the right moment could enhance slow brain waves.

"You can make more of these electrical slow waves through an auditory stimulus, if it comes at just the right time. Similar to a child on a swing, if you push them when they're at the right moment in their movement, you can make that swing go farther," Lewis indicates. "The challenge is: How do you find just the right time?".

How Pink Noise Amplifies Brain Waves.

To test the idea, the team used extremely short bursts of pink noise, each lasting just 50 milliseconds. Pink noise contains the full range of frequencies that humans can hear, much like white noise. However, its lower frequencies are more prominent, while higher frequencies are quieter. The result is a softer, more balanced sound reminiscent of steady rainfall or a waterfall heard from a distance.

It has been revealed that timing was essential. The researchers needed to deliver each burst of sound when a sleeping participant's slow brain waves reached their peak. To identify those moments, they monitored electrical activity using EEG while simultaneously measuring CSF movement with fMRI.

Recent findings suggest that combining the two measurements created a technical obstacle. The powerful magnetic fields used in fMRI interfere with EEG recordings, making it difficult to detect the brain's electrical signals accurately and promptly enough to synchronize the sound.

The team addressed this problem by creating a method that removes interference from EEG signals in less than 100 milliseconds. They also designed an algorithm capable of predicting when the next slow wave peak would occur, compensating for the small delay introduced by processing the signals. Together, these advances made it possible to play each burst of pink noise at the intended moment.

Stronger Brain Cleaning Waves During Sleep.

The researchers tested their approach in 14 healthy volunteers. They found that the carefully timed sounds increased the size of both the brain's slow electrical waves and the accompanying CSF waves. Importantly, the sounds were quiet enough that they did not wake the participants.

The brain scans also helped explain how the process works. Slow electrical waves were associated with blood vessels narrowing and widening, creating a pumping effect that pushes CSF out of the brain. These slow waves occur during non-REM sleep and become increasingly pronounced as sleep deepens.

By enhancing the electrical waves, the researchers were able to strengthen the fluid movement associated with the brain's natural waste removal process. However, the study did not directly establish whether the stronger CSF waves actually removed more waste or improved sleep quality.

Could Pink Noise Improve Sleep and Help Fight Alzheimer's?

The researchers now want to investigate whether increasing CSF flow leads to more refreshing, restorative sleep, particularly for people who struggle with insomnia. Another major goal is to determine whether the technique can improve the brain's ability to clear harmful substances.

It has been revealed that this possibility is especially relevant to Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia, which are associated with the accumulation of abnormal proteins in the brain. If stronger CSF movement ultimately translates into more effective waste removal, the approach could offer a latest way to address one of the biological processes involved in these conditions.

Industry observers note that "Brain waste clearance is really vital for Alzheimer's and other forms of dementia, which are caused, in part, by the buildup of molecules like amyloid and tau in the brain. If we can improve brain waste clearance, we may be able to help prevent the buildups of these plaques that lead to disease," Levitt notes.

The technology could eventually become accessible outside research laboratories. Levitt has launched a company that aims to develop a home device, potentially in the form of a headband, that would deliver sound at the appropriate moments during sleep to increase CSF flow.

For now, the results demonstrate that a simple auditory stimulus, when precisely synchronized with brain activity, can alter the fluid waves associated with the brain's nighttime cleaning process. Whether those changes can translate into better sleep, stronger memory, or protection against neurodegenerative disease remains an vital question for future studies.

The research received funding from a McKnight Scholar Award, a Sloan Fellowship, a Pew Biomedical Scholars Award, the Simons Foundation Collaboration on Plasticity in the Aging Brain, the MIT EECS Transformative Research Fund, the National Institutes of Health, the Corundum Convergence Institute, and the Panasonic Well Fellowship for AI and Wellness.

Jon Hamm and Anna Osceola are officially parents! The "Your Friends & Neighbors" co-stars welcomed their first child together.

The gated property is located at the end of a charming cul-de-sac in the Los Angeles neighborhood, which many big names in Hollywood have called home over the years, including Brad Pitt, Kristen Wiig, and Aubrey Plaza.

It’s not the first time Hamm has invested in the area, purchasing a 3,100-square-foot Los Feliz abode for $900,000 in 2002 with his then-partner, actress Jennifer Westfeldt. The duo parted ways in 2015 after spending 18 years together.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mortgage rates surged higher this week, reversing four consecutive weeks of declines as persistent inflation and geopolitical worries pushed borrowing costs back up.
  • In a recent development, the average rate on 30-year fixed home loans jumped to 7.28% for the week ending Nov.
  • Borrowing costs also remain substantially above where they stood a year ago, when rates averaged 6.26% during the same period in 2025.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mortgage rates surged higher this week, reversing four consecutive weeks of declines as persistent inflation and geopolitical worries pushed borrowing costs back up.

In a recent development, the average rate on 30-year fixed home loans jumped to 7.28% for the week ending Nov. 19, up 17 basis points from 7.11% recorded the week before, according to Freddie Mac.

Borrowing costs also remain substantially above where they stood a year ago, when rates averaged 6.26% during the same period in 2025.

So what does this mean for homebuyers? Using the Realtor.com® mortgage calculator, we can look at how the math works out for the median-priced home in the U.S.

All examples assume a 30-year fixed mortgage and include principal and interest only, excluding property taxes, homeowners insurance, and mortgage insurance.

For a homebuyer eyeing the median house price of $430,000, a 20% down payment results in a loan amount of $344,000.

At today's 7.28% rate, the monthly principal and interest payment is approximately $2,354. This reflects a $40 monthly increase from the previous week’s payment of $2,314.

Compared to the 6.26% average from November 2025, which required a $2,120 monthly payment for a home at this price, today’s buyers are paying $234 more a month.

The monthly costs have also risen markedly for those using FHA loans with a 3.5% down payment.

According to recent reports, on a $430,000 home, an FHA borrower would finance roughly $414,950. At today’s 7.28% rate, the monthly principal and interest payment comes to approximately $2,839.

Sources indicate that this reflects a $48 increase from last week's monthly cost of $2,791. Compared to the 6.26% rates of November 2025, where the monthly payment for this loan amount sat at $2,558, today’s FHA borrowers are paying an extra $281 in interest every month.

However, looking back at the October 2023 peak of 7.79%, where the payment for a home at this price reached $2,984, today's monthly payment still offers $145 in relief.

The long-term financial picture indicates how this abrupt reversal affects total borrowing costs over a 30-year term.

A buyer with a 20% down payment at today’s 7.28% rate will pay a total of $847,328 in principal and interest over the life of the mortgage.

While this week's jump erased much of the ground gained over the past month, this total still represents a contrast to the October 2023 peak of 7.79%, when the total cost for that same $344,000 loan would have reached $890,630.

By securing a mortgage at today’s rate instead of that peak, a homebuyer effectively avoids $43,302 in interest charges over the 30-year loan life.

In a recent development, FHA borrowers see a similar trajectory of long-term figures. Financing the current median-priced home at today's 7.28% rate results in a lifetime payment of $1,022,090 for principal and interest.

Sources indicate that if that same loan had been locked in at the 7.79% peak in late 2023, the total cost would have climbed to $1,074,323. This represents a total long-term savings of $52,233 for FHA buyers.

Own, don’t rent: Why agentic AI is pulling cloud computing back on-prem

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (822 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, agentic AI is reviving an argument over renting versus owning compute, and the model plane — the layer that decides where AI models run — sits at the center of it.
  • That shift favors companies that built early for on-premises cloud infrastructure.
  • According to recent reports, “Cloud computing is great, but the model shouldn’t be exclusively to rent it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 12:46 EST / NOVEMBER 20 2026.

In a recent development, agentic AI is reviving an argument over renting versus owning compute, and the model plane — the layer that decides where AI models run — sits at the center of it. Open-source efforts such as Upbound Inc.’s Modelplane route inference across clouds, but many enterprises want the models on hardware they control.

That shift favors companies that built early for on-premises cloud infrastructure. Oxide Computer Co., which raised $445 million in October to expand rack production, built its business on the idea that enterprises at scale will want to own their computers, according to Bryan Cantrill (pictured), co-founder and chief technology officer at Oxide.

According to recent reports, “Cloud computing is great, but the model shouldn’t be exclusively to rent it. You get to a certain scale, as it turns out, you want to own your own computer,” Cantrill remarked.

Industry observers note that cantrill spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed renting versus owning compute, why agentic workloads are moving on-prem and multi-tenancy for isolating those workloads.

Sources indicate that agentic workloads are driving an explosion in compute demand, and much of it is CPU-heavy work that enterprises would rather own than rent. Economics remains the main reason to bring it in-house, but where models live is a close second, Cantrill explained. That makes the model plane as much a data governance decision as an infrastructure one.

“There is a real enterprise drive towards open-weight models, and I think you’re going to see more and more of that as people want to run the models on-prem and allow their data to not actually leave,” Cantrill mentioned.

Industry observers note that security is the other half. Oxide stripped the UEFI BIOS and baseboard management controller out of its rack to shrink the attack surface, and built public cloud-grade multi-tenancy in from the start. Those early design choices give enterprises a perimeter for isolating agentic workloads, according to Cantrill.

According to recent reports, “I think multi-tenancy means you’ve got potentially adversarial tenants that are going to be on the same resource,” Cantrill said. “They’re going to be sharing the same computer, sharing the same network, and they need to do that … without violating the confidentiality, without breaching one another.”.

In a recent development, the same racks can take on legacy virtualization workloads from customers unhappy with pricing changes at Broadcom Inc.’s VMware business. That lets enterprises run old and fresh applications on one general-purpose platform, Cantrill noted.

“You want all that flexibility that you get from elastic compute, but you need it for economic reasons, security reasons, latency reasons,” Cantrill mentioned of the case for on-premises cloud computing. “You need it in your own data center. You want to control your fate.”.

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1602 w)

Latest Update: The Houses That Made New Orleans—and the Rising Cost of Keeping Them Standing

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1602 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The World Monuments Fund's 2026 Irreplaceable America list recognizes the kind of architecture that has come to define the country—landmarks that serve as reminders of who we are and where we came from.
  • But one place was so emblematic of the country's past, present, and future that no single building could serve as a symbol of the whole.
  • New Orleans is the only entire city among the 10 places to receive the designation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The World Monuments Fund's 2026 Irreplaceable America list recognizes the kind of architecture that has come to define the country—landmarks that serve as reminders of who we are and where we came from.

But one place was so emblematic of the country's past, present, and future that no single building could serve as a symbol of the whole.

New Orleans is the only entire city among the 10 places to receive the designation.

“Latest Orleans itself is irreplaceable—not just one building, one district or one monument, but the entire living city,” claims Kristin Gisleson Palmer, executive director of the Preservation Resource Center of New Orleans when the title was unveiled.

Yet the buildings that earned the city that recognition now face a mounting threat: the cost of protecting them.

Sources indicate that newly introduced Orleans has the second-highest homeowners insurance costs relative to property values among the nation's 100 largest metro areas, according to research from Realtor.com®. Now, as storms intensify and insurance costs rise, the city's historic homes are becoming more expensive to protect and preserve.

Recent findings suggest that on a recent walking tour through Bayou St. John, Heather Veneziano—director of Tulane University's Historic Preservation Program, who helped spearhead the city's nomination—began not with a building, but with the ground beneath our feet.

The bayou that gives the neighborhood its name connects to Lake Pontchartrain, a brackish estuary fed by rivers and linked to the Gulf of Mexico. The slower-moving waters served Indigenous communities as a transportation route before European colonization.

Alongside that access, nearby natural ridges offered comparatively high ground in a landscape shaped by water, making the area an appealing, if imperfect, place to settle.

Recent findings suggest that but higher ground didn't always mean dry ground. And the European settlers who followed knew the water would eventually return, and they built their homes accordingly.

“You have to build for place,” Veneziano tells Realtor.com.

Sources indicate that at the Pitot House, a Creole colonial country house built in 1799, she pointed to the elevated living quarters as an example. The ground level, she noted, could be used for storage during dry seasons, while allowing floodwater to enter below the principal rooms during wet ones.

“You lived, I think, with the knowledge that water is going to be a thing you can't fight against,” Veneziano said.

Sources indicate that that understanding shaped the building from the ground up. Its broad roof and galleries offered shelter from the elements, while its timber framing incorporated cypress, a locally abundant wood prized for its resistance to decay and insects.

Residents adapted that approach across generations, raising homes as upcoming neighborhoods and architectural forms developed, according to FEMA's history of building elevation in New Orleans.

But even the most carefully adapted homes can't eliminate the danger.

Today, an estimated 88.9% of residential property value in the Fresh Orleans–Metairie metro faces severe or extreme flood risk, according to the 2025 Housing and Climate Risk Report from Realtor.com.

As Latest Orleans grew, new residents brought their own architectural traditions, transforming both the appearance of its neighborhoods and the ways people lived within them.

The Creole townhouse, with shops beneath upper-floor residences and courtyards tucked behind masonry facades, became a defining feature of the French Quarter.

Interestingly, its appearance was partly shaped by disaster. After fires destroyed much of the city in 1788 and 1794, Spanish authorities favored more fire-resistant construction, helping establish the brick, stucco, and ironwork associated with the neighborhood today.

Upcoming Orleans' celebrated architecture was also built on slavery.

Sources indicate that behind the ornate facades, enslaved people lived in courtyard quarters and worked in the homes they helped construct. Enslaved craftspeople helped construct the homes themselves, while the city's wealth was deeply tied to their forced labor.

According to recent reports, yet within this slaveholding society, free Black Upcoming Orleanians also established themselves as builders and property owners. Architectural historian Tara A. Dudley has documented how the Dolliole and Soulié families shaped the city's housing and built wealth through real estate, despite laws restricting Black economic independence.

Industry observers note that following the Louisiana Purchase in 1803, Anglo-American settlers introduced different architectural preferences. Wealthy merchants built double-gallery houses Uptown, their stacked porches and classical columns reflecting fortunes tied to shipping, cotton, and enslaved peoples.

The craftsmanship that distinguished these homes also presents a modern financial challenge.

Rami Sneineh, a licensed insurance producer and owner of Insurance Navy Brokers, indicates replacing handmade windows, woodwork, or plaster may require scarce materials and specialized craftspeople.

“If your home sustained significant damage, it could take months to source similar materials and you’d likely need to hire specialized craftsmen to restore those one-of-a-kind details,” he claims.

An older home worth $400,000, he offers as a hypothetical example, might cost $700,000 to reconstruct with comparable details.

But not every architectural tradition emerged from wealth.

Recent findings suggest that the shotgun house, which spread through working-class neighborhoods during the 19th century, arranged narrow rooms one behind another. Its origins are debated, but historians have identified possible African and Caribbean influences. Double shotguns accommodated two households beneath one roof, making efficient use of narrow lots.

According to recent reports, and as drainage technology opened lower-lying areas to development, raised-basement houses appeared in neighborhoods such as Broadmoor and Mid-City. Their main living quarters sat a full story above the ground, carrying the tradition of elevation into the 20th century.

Yet the pumping systems that enabled the city's expansion also contributed to land subsidence, according to the Historic New Orleans Collection.

The homes remained elevated, but their protection increasingly depended on an engineered system of drainage, pumps, and levees—whose vulnerabilities became devastatingly apparent during Hurricane Katrina.

According to recent reports, as we walked through Bayou St. John, the distant sound of a marching band practicing for upcoming Mardi Gras parades drifted across the neighborhood. Veneziano paused to listen, reflecting on the communities hidden behind and whithin the structures that surrounded us.

“The architecture is the setting for those relationships,” she mentioned. “And people's voices are told through the built environment in which they live.”.

Today, Fresh Orleans has 26 historic districts listed on the National Register of Historic Places, covering more than 45,000 properties and roughly 40% of its urbanized area.

But preserving the appearance of those neighborhoods doesn't always preserve the communities within them.

During our walk, Veneziano pointed out double shotguns converted into single-family homes, a trend she said accelerated after Hurricane Katrina. The exteriors might remain recognizable even as two residences become one.

“It's taking away affordable housing for the rental population because there's not as many rental units anymore,” she said.

The lost rental unit also means losing a potential source of income that could help an owner maintain an aging structure.

And for the homeowners who do remain, those costs are rising on many fronts.

Single-family homes in the area carry an estimated annual homeowners insurance premium of $8,328, according to research from Realtor.com—equivalent to 3.6% of its median market value, and the second-highest burden among the 100 largest metropolitan areas.

Those estimates don't even account for the specialized demands of restoring historic architecture or purchasing separate flood coverage.

Recent findings suggest that even insured owners can face substantial out of pocket expenses. Sneineh notes that a 5% hurricane deductible on a home insured for $600,000 leaves an owner responsible for $30,000 before the insurer covers eligible damage.

“Properties that were previously affordable to purchase may now be unaffordable to insure,” says Mujahid Merchant, an independent researcher in climate risk and mortgage credit.

When private coverage becomes unavailable, homeowners may turn to Louisiana Citizens, the state's insurer of last resort, which is required to charge higher rates than qualifying private insurers.

Sources indicate that and if a mortgaged home loses required coverage, its lender may purchase more expensive insurance and charge the owner. Merchant warns that the resulting increase in monthly payments can contribute to delinquency or foreclosure.

Yet some of the solutions draw on the same practical ingenuity that shaped these homes in the first place.

“Contrary to popular belief, you can strengthen your historic home’s roof without changing its historic look,” Sneineh states.

Louisiana's Fortify Homes Program offers eligible owners grants of up to $10,000 to strengthen roofs against hurricane winds. A state report found that median recipients saved $1,250 a year, or 22%, on insurance premiums. Latest Orleans also provides an expedited review process for qualifying roof replacements in local historic districts.

But even as owners find latest ways to protect their homes from the elements, keeping those buildings affordable presents a different challenge.

Sources indicate that after Hurricane Katrina, thousands of Latest Orleanians left for cities such as Houston and Atlanta. Not everyone returned.

Veneziano described the familiarity of living near former teachers, relatives, and neighbors whose lives have intertwined for generations—connections that can't simply be reconstructed in another place.

According to recent reports, “You can't take what you have anywhere and put it somewhere else,” she remarked. “Places don't matter without people.".

AI deals shrink to as little as 30 days as the data layer sets the pace
